pages.title: The import page
pages.html:
The import page sets up a project. A project consists of one or more IDEAS exports, the names and roles of their channels, and the analysis settings. From this page you also run the analysis and view the overview of the results. Start it with uv run imagestream or uv run imagestream-cli gui. The page opens in your browser at once, with a spinner while the program loads its analysis modules (up to about 20 s on a first start). It is served by the program on your own computer, so no data leave your computer.

The page remembers the last saved project. Save settings, Run and Quit all save the project. If you reload the page before saving, the browser restores the unsaved setup and shows a message about it. If you start the program a second time, it opens the page that is already running. Quit (top right) saves the project and stops the program. If you don't quit, the program stops by itself 15 minutes after the page was closed, but never during a run.

The ? button next to a step or a group of settings, and the Help button at the top, open the matching part of this manual in a panel at the side. Pressing F1 or ? does the same for the step under the mouse pointer.

1. Project

Choose the output folder of the project here, or click Browse… to choose a folder. The results of each dataset go to <project>/<experiment>/<dataset>/.

The top bar has Load settings…, which opens an existing project.toml, and Save settings, which writes the project file (project.toml in the output folder) without running the analysis. A second Save settings button sits at the bottom of the page, so that you don't have to scroll back up after changing the settings.

2. IDEAS exports

Click Add zip files… to add exports, or paste the path of a zip file and click Add. For each export, set the following:

  • Pixel size: choose 20×, 40× or 60× (1, 0.5 or 0.33 µm per pixel), or other… to type a value. The IDEAS files don't contain the pixel size, so you have to set it. These are the nominal values; check them for your instrument.
  • Datasets: each first-level folder in the zip is one dataset, listed in a table. Tick Use to include a dataset in the analysis. Objects shows how many objects the dataset contains, and Complete how many of them have an image for every channel that is needed; incomplete objects are left out. Experiment groups datasets that are classified together (see Pools below); it starts as the name of the zip. Condition (for example control or treated) and Replicate (the donor or independent experiment the dataset comes from) are needed only if you want to compare conditions; see Comparing conditions.

  • Channels: the example images show a few objects in each channel. Give every channel that is needed a name, and tick its role:

    Role Meaning How many
    BF brightfield one
    Tumor the tumor-cell marker one
    Immune an immune-cell marker; if there are several, they are summed one or more
    Subtype an immune subtype marker; each cell is called positive or negative for it none or more
    MOI a marker of interest, which is measured along the membrane one or more, or none

    A channel can have two roles, for example a subtype marker that is also a marker of interest. With several markers of interest, the membrane enrichment is measured for each of them in the same way (see Several markers of interest). Without a marker of interest, the analysis gives only the cell types, subtypes and contacts. In that case, leave MOI unticked and switch Membrane profiles and enrichment off.

    When two or more exports have been added, a Copy setup to all button appears at the bottom of each export's card, below the channel table. It copies the pixel size and the channel names of that export to the other exports. The roles follow the names (see below), so they need no copying.

Remove, in the title bar of an export, removes the export from the project, but not from the disk.

Technical: roles go with the name

The roles are stored once for the whole project, by marker name ([channels] in project.toml). Each export only maps its channel numbers to names. As a result, exports of the same panel whose channels are numbered differently (because of another instrument setup or another IDEAS template) need no separate roles, only the right names. A role tick box is grayed out until the channel has a name. When you rename a channel, its roles move to the new name, unless another export still uses the old name.

Projects written before November 2026 stored the roles per export, by channel number. When such a project is opened, the roles are converted to roles by name if all exports agree. Otherwise, each export keeps its own roles by number, which are shown under its channel table.

3. Analysis settings

These settings apply to all datasets of the project. The most important ones are:

  • Tumor / immune markers: nuclear or membrane. This tells the program where the tumor and immune markers stain, which determines how the image for Cellpose is made (see Segmentation).
  • Python with Cellpose, Model and Cell diameter (px) control the segmentation. Python with Cellpose can be the python.exe of an environment or the folder of that environment (a venv, conda or pixi environment, or a project folder with .venv or .pixi in it). A chip in the heading of Segmentation (Cellpose) shows what the program found there: in green the Cellpose version and the name of the GPU, or a warning when Cellpose is missing or no GPU was found (Cellpose then runs on the processor, which is much slower). The check runs in the background each time the page opens. Sizes are given in pixels; see Segmentation for how to convert them from µm. Reuse the previous Cellpose result if nothing changed (on by default) skips Cellpose for a dataset when its Cellpose input and settings are the same as in its previous run.
  • Classify together, Threshold of the subtype markers and Artefact control how the cell types are assigned. Thresholds set by hand lists the thresholds that were applied from a dashboard; Automatic again removes them.

  • Membrane profiles and enrichment and the membrane pairs control the membrane enrichment. Every marker of interest has a row of its own, for example Marker: membrane of … interface with …, so that each marker can be measured on its own pair. The rows follow the MOI ticks in step 2: a marker that you tick gets a row, and a marker that you untick loses its row and its pair. A renamed channel keeps its pair. Without a marker of interest there are no rows. Membrane of and Interface with are menus. Their first choice is automatic: where the marker is expressed means the cell type that carries the marker of interest, which the program finds in the data for each marker, and the other cell type means the other one. The other choices are the tumor cells, all immune cells, every combination of the subtype markers ticked in step 2 (for example immune A+ cells or immune negative cells), and with two or more subtype markers each marker on its own (immune cells A+ (any other markers)). These are the same choices as in the dashboard's membrane card, which shows only the combinations that occur in the data. The menus follow the roles: when you tick, untick or rename a subtype marker, they change with it. A pair that you choose applies to that marker only, and each side on its own: if you choose only Membrane of, Interface with stays automatic. The run check asks for at least one MOI channel when Membrane profiles and enrichment is on.

    A value that the menus do not offer, for example from an older project or a settings file edited by hand, is kept and shown as its own choice, marked (from the settings file), so that saving the project does not change it. If it is not a selection of the panel, the list above the Run button says so, with the likely meaning: for example, Immune A is no subset, and the program asks whether you meant A+ (every A-positive immune cell) or Immune A+ (A positive only). The run does not start until you choose a pair in the menu. A valid subset that has no cells in a dataset only gives a warning in the log, and that dataset gets no membrane files for it.

    In project.toml the pairs are tables by marker name, for example [membrane.pairs.'Marker'] with cells = ['Tumor'] and partners = ['Immune Subtype A+']; the menus write one entry per side, or none for the automatic choice. An older project with one pair for all markers (membrane.cells and membrane.partners) is shown with that pair in the row of every marker, and saved as one entry per marker.

All settings lists every setting with its default value.

Pools

The setting Classify together (one set of thresholds) has two options. With experiment (the default), the cells of all datasets with the same experiment label are classified together. As a result, "positive for a marker" means the same in every dataset of that experiment. With dataset, each dataset is classified on its own. See Cell types.

4. Run

The list above Run all datasets names anything that is still missing, such as an output folder, a pixel size, or a channel for a role. For the immune-cell markers, one ticked Immune channel in each export is enough: the markers are summed, so an export may lack a marker that another export has. The button works only when this list is empty. The run first saves the project. If a dataset fails, the error is logged and the other datasets are still analyzed. For a dataset of 2000 cells or more, the membrane profiles are measured in several processes at once (up to eight processor cores), so the computer can be busy for a while during that step.

While a run is going on, a blue bar under the button says Running…, with a progress bar, the dataset in progress (Dataset 2 of 3, or Measuring / Finishing dataset 2 of 3 when the datasets of an experiment are classified together) and the time so far. The same state is shown next to the title of step 5. Run all datasets reads Running… and, like every other Run and Run again button, cannot be clicked until the run ends. Stop ends the run. The log below shows the details. At the end, the bar shows one of:

  • Done (green): every dataset of the run was analyzed, and the overview is up to date.
  • Done, N of M failed (red): the run finished, but some datasets failed. Their rows in the overview show the error.
  • Stopped (red): you clicked Stop. Datasets that the run had not finished keep their previous results, marked previous run in the overview.
  • Failed (exit code N) (red): the run itself stopped with an error. The log says why.

To run one dataset (again), click Run in its row of the dataset table in step 2, or Run again in its row of the overview. The other datasets keep their results, and the overview is written again from all of them. With Classify together set to experiment, a dataset is classified together with the other datasets of its experiment. Its whole experiment then runs, so that all of them keep one set of thresholds; the tooltip of the button says so. Cellpose is skipped for every dataset whose Cellpose input and settings have not changed.

5. Overview

The overview shows one row per analyzed dataset, with links to its dashboard and its folder. Below the table, it shows the partner preference of each experiment and, if the datasets have conditions, the comparison of the conditions. During a run, the rows that are being computed again are greyed out and marked running…, and they are refreshed as soon as their dataset is done. See The project overview.

pages.title: The dashboard
pages.html:
Every analyzed dataset gets a dashboard.html file in its folder. You can open it from the overview of the import page, or directly from disk by double-clicking it. It needs no server and no internet connection, so you can send the folder to a colleague. The event images are stored in the dashboard_files/ folder next to it.

All views on the page are linked. When you hover over a cell in the events, in a plot or in a table, it is highlighted in every view. Clicking a cell selects it and shows it in the Cell card. Clicking an event next to its cells selects the event and shows it in the Cell card. Press Esc to clear the selection. To select a cell or an event when the page opens, add #cell=12 or #event=5 to the address, as in dashboard.html#cell=12; the cell number is its row in the cell table.

The page remembers its view in the browser, separately for each dashboard: the channels and their brightness, the overlays, the filter, the sort order, the size, the magnification in the Cell card, the marker of interest and the membrane pair of each marker, the scale of the membrane histograms and the open tabs. The next time you open the dashboard, it shows the same view again.

Top: counts and filters

The header shows the number of events, cells, cell types, events with one tumor cell and one immune cell, touching pairs, artefacts and cells with an interface. The filter row below the header applies to every view:

  • Events: shows all events, the events with immune cells and tumor cells, the events with one tumor cell and one immune cell, the events with an interface, or the events with touching cells. When you choose a contact in the interaction matrix, a chip for it is added here; click ✕ to remove it.
  • Sort: sets the order of the events.
  • Size: sets the size of the event images. You can also hold Ctrl and scroll over the gallery. Small event images show only their event number; hover over one to see its IDEAS object number.

The ? button after a heading, and the ? Help button at the top, open the part of this manual that describes that item in a panel at the side of the page. F1 or ? does the same for the card under the mouse pointer. The help panel also works offline.

Events

This card shows the events as a gallery. Each cell is outlined in the color of its cell type, and the interfaces are drawn in aqua. Only the events that are visible on the screen are drawn, so the page stays fast for large datasets. The selected event has a dark frame and a bold number. The gallery takes the full height of the card, as tall as the cards on the right.

Channels and overlays

The column to the left of the gallery controls what is drawn in the event images:

  • Channels: one row per channel, with a tick box to show or hide the channel and a control for its brightness. Double-click the name of a channel to show only that channel. The brightfield channel starts at half brightness, underneath the fluorescence channels.
  • Overlays: the outlines of the cells (in the color of their cell type), the interfaces, and the contacts. A contact is drawn as a white line with a dark edge between the centers of two cells that touch.

Cell

This card shows the selected cell: its event, its measurements, its subtype markers (the value, and whether it is positive or negative), and the cells it touches. If the membrane analysis was run, the card also shows the membrane profile of the cell, aligned on the interface. With several markers of interest, the membrane rows and the profile are those of the marker chosen in the Membrane enrichment card, and the row marker names it.

When an event is selected but no cell, the card shows that event: its object number, its cells and their types, the number of touching pairs, and the marker of interest at the interface and on the rest of the membrane, from the per-event table (of the marker chosen in the membrane card). You can hover over the cells in the enlarged image and click one to show it.

The − and + buttons under the image set its magnification: 100 % is one screen pixel per image pixel, and the steps are 100, 150, 200, 300, 400 and 600 %. The default is 200 %. The page remembers the last magnification.

Below the measurements, a montage shows the event once per loaded channel, in grey, at half the magnification of the large image (at least 100 %). Each channel is shown with its own display range, whether or not it is switched on in Channels, so you can see what every marker shows on its own. The colour square in front of the name is the colour of the channel in the composite; hover over the name to see the channel number, its role and its display range. The selected cell is outlined in white.

If the membrane analysis was run, tick membrane band next to the magnification, or press the space bar, to lay the membrane band over the large image and the montage, semi-transparent. The band is the strip of pixels that was straightened and measured. It is Straightening width pixels wide, and centred where the membrane lies (by default) or on the smoothed outline (Band centred on: outline). With Straighten inside the measured cell only, only the part inside the cell is shown. Its colour says what each position along the membrane counts as, for the membrane pair of the membrane card:

Colour Meaning
aqua the interface with a partner of the pair
amber the free membrane, which touches no cell: the reference that the interface is compared with
grey a contact with a cell outside the pair: left out of both

For a selected cell, the band of that cell is shown. A cell of the partner type shows its contacts with the measured cells as interface. For a selected event, the bands of the measured cells of the pair are shown. A line under the montage repeats the colours and the width. The space bar does nothing while you type in a field or when a menu or a button has the focus. The page remembers whether the band is shown.

Subtype markers

This card is shown when the panel has subtype markers. For each marker, it shows a histogram of the immune cells on a log scale, log(intensity − min + 1), with the threshold of the run as a dashed line and a slider. The bars have the color of the marker's channel, and the numbers under the histogram are background-subtracted intensities. If the histogram has two clear peaks, the threshold belongs in the gap between them (see Cell types). Dragging a slider changes the subtypes everywhere on the page: the colors, the plots, the contacts, the membrane pairs and the tables. The count next to the marker shows how many immune cells are positive.

While you drag, the events, the cell classes and the count follow at once. The contacts, the membrane enrichment and the tables take longer to compute on large datasets, so they follow when you release the slider, or when it has stood still for 0.7 s.

The sliders change only the page. To use their thresholds in the tables and in every other output, there are two ways:

  • Apply to the project… is available only in a dashboard that was opened from the overview of the import page. It writes the thresholds that you moved, and the membrane pair if you changed it, into the project, and then runs the project again. Cellpose is skipped when its input and settings have not changed, so this takes only seconds per dataset. The page reloads when the run has finished. The thresholds apply to all datasets of the project, so the page first asks for confirmation and says how many datasets will be affected.
  • Copy as settings copies the thresholds and the membrane pair to the clipboard, as lines for a settings file or for project.toml, and also shows them on the page. This also works in a dashboard that was opened from disk.

A threshold that was set in this way shows Run: manual under its slider, together with an automatic button. If you click automatic, the threshold is computed automatically again on the next Apply. The import page lists the thresholds that were set by hand under Analysis settings. Reset all returns all sliders to the thresholds of the run.

Technical: what the slider changes, and what not

The slider applies the new threshold to the immune cells on the page. It does not repeat the clustering into tumor cells and immune cells, and the artefacts stay as they were computed, because both would need the whole classification to be run again. (The artefact rule uses thresholds over all detections; see Cell types.) In the run, a threshold that was set by hand (classification.thresholds) is used for both the subtypes and the artefact rule.

A threshold that is applied to the project can therefore change the artefacts too, and with them the numbers of the other cells.

Cell classes

This plot shows the area of each cell against its marker ratio (immune marker / tumor marker), on log–log axes. This is the space in which k-means separates the tumor cells from the immune cells. Click a cell type in the legend to bring its points to the front.

Interactions

  • Partner preference (left): the rows are cell types, and the columns are the cell types they touch. The color and the number in each square give the number of observed contacts divided by the number expected by chance, within the events with three or more cells. Blue means fewer contacts than expected by chance, and red means more. The fraction touching option shows instead the share of the row's cells that touch at least one cell of the column's type. Hover over a square to see the counts. Click a square to show only the events with that contact, with the contacts drawn.
  • Among immune cells (tab): the subset preference. For each immune subtype, it shows whether that subtype is the one that touches the tumor cell (or another subtype) more often than expected by chance, in events that offer a choice. A square is colored only where the 95 % interval excludes 1. Hover over a square to see the counts and the interval.
  • Both matrices leave out the cell types that have nothing to show: no contact, and none expected (with fraction touching: no contact at all). This happens with rare combinations of subtype markers. The note under the matrix names them, with their number of cells; Show them puts them back (with empty squares), Hide them leaves them out again.
  • Share of contacts (right): for each cell type, which cell types it touches, as a share of its contacts or as numbers. On the right, it also shows the share of its cells that touch any other cell.

Cell contacts explains how contacts and chance are defined, and what they can and cannot tell you.

Membrane enrichment

This card is shown when the membrane analysis was run. The Membrane of and interface with menus choose the pair of cells to compare. Each can be a cell type, an immune subtype, or all immune cells that are positive for a marker. The page computes the enrichment for the chosen pair immediately. Apply to the project… makes it the pair that is used for the tables (see Subtype markers).

With two or more markers of interest, a Marker menu comes first. It switches the whole card to that marker: the histograms, the profile, the heatmap, All pairs, the badge, the membrane columns of the Cells table and the cell card. Each marker starts with the pair of the run, which is by default the cell type that carries that marker against the other type, and keeps the pair you choose for it. The line under the menus names the marker and the cell type that carries it. Apply to the project… and Copy as settings write the pair of the marker shown only ([membrane.pairs.'<marker>']); the other markers keep theirs. The page remembers the chosen marker.

  • Histogram: the enrichment at the interface (aqua) of every cell with an interface, compared with random control windows on cells without an interface (dashed), in the measure chosen (below): by default the log2 ratio of the interface and the free membrane, that is, the membrane that touches no other cell (1 = twice as bright). The histograms start at −2 for the log2 ratio, and at −5 SD for the SD scores. By default the scale is automatic: the maximum is the 99th percentile of the interface values or of the control windows, whichever is higher, so that one extreme cell does not squeeze the rest into a few bins. The bin width is chosen to give at most 60 bins. Use the − and + buttons under the plot to change the maximum or the bin width, and auto to return to the automatic scale. The page redraws the histograms immediately and remembers the scale. Values above the maximum are not counted; the note under the plot says how many cells that concerns.
  • Average profile: the average membrane profile of the cells with an interface, with the interface at 0 µm (as in the heatmap and the cell card). Its vertical axis fits the curve, so a small enrichment is not flattened.
  • Heatmap: one row per cell with an interface, with the strongest enrichment at the top. The colour scale is ±6 SD for the SD scores; for the log2 ratio it is set from the rows shown (the legend gives it). The stripe under it shows the rows averaged per position, on the same colour scale (the average profile as a colour band); hover over it to read the value and the number of cells at that position.
  • Across the membrane: where the band lies (folded): the marker of interest averaged across the outline of the measured cells, at the free membrane (amber) and at the contacts with the partners' cell type (aqua), in µm from the outline (− inside the cell). The strips under the axis show the band of each. By default each band is centred on the peak of its curve; with Band centred on: cell each cell has a place of its own around it (the note says how many); with the band on the outline, both strips are centred on 0, and a strip that covers less of the amber peak than of the aqua one makes the interface look enriched without cause. See Where the membrane lies.
  • All pairs (folded): the median enrichment of every combination of Membrane of and interface with, with the number of cells and the marker check of each pair. Use this table to compare pairs (see The control). Click a number to show that pair.
  • Measure: how the interface is scored. log2 ratio to own membrane (the default) compares the interface with the cell's own membrane that touches no cell, as a fold change: 0 = as bright, 1 = twice as bright. log2 ratio above same-type contacts subtracts the median of the measured cells at contacts with cells of their own kind, for a marker that the partners carry too; a dashed line in the average profile marks that reference. SD above own membrane and SD above same-type contacts are the same in standard deviations of the free membrane (the macro's score). SD above both membranes (experimental) also subtracts the partner's free membrane at every interface point; it failed its own check on real data. The histograms, the heatmap, All pairs, the cell card and the Cells table follow the choice, and the page remembers it. Ways to score an interface explains when to use which.
  • Across the band: maximum (the default, as the macro and the tables) takes the brightest sample across the membrane at every position; sum adds all samples. At an interface both membranes lie in the band, and only the sum adds them up, as SD above both membranes assumes. Everything in the card follows the switch; the tables of the output folder keep the maximum. The page remembers it.
  • The badge next to the menus shows where the marker of interest is expressed: on the measured cells, also on their partners, on both at a similar level, or hardly on the measured cells at all (gray: not informative). Before you trust a result with an amber, red or gray badge, read Membrane enrichment. The control explains what the control windows can and cannot tell you.
Technical: the page and the tables

The page computes the pair from the membrane profile and the neighbor track of every cell, in the same way as the program does for the tables. Only the random control windows differ: the page uses a fixed seed, and the run uses an unseeded random generator. Their summaries agree closely. The tables (Membrane intensity analysis - <marker>.tsv, one per marker of interest) hold the pair of the run: the pair set in the settings, or by default the cell type that carries the marker against the other type.

The per-event measure of the Fiji macro (the marker at the interface against the rest of the membrane, per event) is no longer plotted: the pair comparisons supersede it. Its values are still in the Events table, in the sort membrane ratio and in All cell combinations.tsv.

Tables

The Cells, Events and Contacts tables can be sorted by clicking a column header. The rows follow the filters, and at most 2000 rows are shown; sort the table to see other rows. Download .tsv saves the current table with all its rows, filtered and sorted as on the page, and with the subtypes set by the sliders. The tables of the run itself are the TSV files in the output folder.

pages.title: The project overview
pages.html:
The last step of the import page shows the project overview. It has one row per analyzed dataset. Below the table, it shows the partner preference of every experiment and, when the datasets have a condition and a replicate, the comparison of the conditions. The same information is written to overview.tsv, interactions.tsv and condition comparison.tsv in the project folder. Only the datasets of the project count (see During and after a run).

The table

The table has one row per dataset. The Dashboard button opens the dashboard of the dataset, Folder opens its folder, and Run again runs only that dataset again (see Run). For a dataset that failed, the row shows the error instead. Hover over a column header to see what the column means:

Column Meaning
events, cells the number of events analyzed; the number of cells after the clean-up, including artefacts
immune cells, tumor cells, artefacts the number of cells of each type (see Cell types)
single tumor + single immune cell the number of events with exactly one tumor cell and one immune cell that touch
interactions the number of pairs of touching cells, of any cell types
tumor–immune contacts the number of pairs of a tumor cell and an immune cell that touch
doublet fraction single tumor + single immune cell divided by events
immune negative, immune A+, immune A+ B+, … the number of immune cells with exactly that combination of positive subtype markers (immune A+ cells are negative for the other markers); 0 when a dataset has none

Then come the columns of each marker of interest. Their names end in the name of the marker, for example MOI on (Marker):

Column Meaning
MOI on the cell type (Tumor or Immune) that carries the marker, found in the data; by default its membranes are measured (see A pair of cell types)
MOI partners / measured the marker check (see Membrane enrichment)
marker check the marker check of the marker's membrane pair, in words
median Tumor (or Immune) membrane ratio, doublets computed in the events of single tumor + single immune cell, for the cell type that carries the marker: the mean of the marker in that cell's membrane band at the interface, divided by that in the rest of its band. This is the macro's ratio. It uses all partners of the other type, whatever the membrane pair, and has no control; see the per-event table
membrane pair the pair that the enrichment columns after it describe: Membrane of … with …
membranes, with interface the number of measured cells of that pair, and how many of them touch a partner
median log2 ratio, median control log2 ratio (windows) the median enrichment of the cells with an interface, as the log2 ratio of the interface and the free membrane (1 = twice as bright), and that of the control windows (about 0); the main readout
median stdDevs above mean, median control (windows) the same in standard deviations of the free membrane (the macro's score)

The enrichment columns describe the membrane pair of each marker. If you click Apply to the project… in a dashboard with another pair selected, they describe that pair, so always note the pair together with the numbers. Every other pair of every dataset is in membrane pairs.tsv in the project folder, so you don't need another run to see them.

During and after a run

The overview reads the results that are in the project folder. While a run is going on, some of them are about to be replaced, so a column before experiment shows the state of each row:

State Meaning
running… (greyed out) the run is computing this dataset again; until it is done, the values are those of the previous run
running… (greyed out, no links) the run is computing this dataset for the first time; there are no results yet
updated written by the last run
previous run (greyed out) the last run was stopped or failed before it reached this dataset; the values come from an earlier run, with the settings of that time
not in the project (greyed out) see below

The overview is refreshed every time a dataset is done, and once more at the end. The partner preference and the comparison of conditions are computed at the end of a run, so during a run they are greyed out with a note.

Results that are not part of the project. If you reuse an output folder, it can hold result folders of datasets that are no longer in the project: a dataset that was removed or unticked in step 2, or one whose experiment label was changed (its results go to a folder named after the experiment). These results are left out of the overview, of overview.tsv, of the partner preference and of the comparison. A line under the table says how many there are, and Show them lists them, greyed out and marked not in the project. Their files stay on disk: delete those folders yourself if you no longer need them.

Partner preference per experiment

For each experiment, a matrix shows the contacts observed divided by the contacts expected by chance, for all its datasets together. Only events with three or more cells are used. Blue means fewer contacts than chance, and red means more. Hover over a square to see the counts. Comparing the matrices of different experiments shows whether a preference holds across samples.

Between immune subtypes, read the subset preference instead, for two reasons. First, this matrix also compares cells of different sizes, so immune–immune ratios well below 1 can appear without any preference. Second, it pools the datasets of the experiment, so it cannot show a difference between conditions within that experiment. Cell contacts explains how the matrix is computed and what it does not measure.

Comparing conditions

When the datasets have a Condition and a Replicate (set in step 2), this section tests whether the subset preference and the membrane enrichment differ between conditions, across the replicates. Use Compare with to choose the reference condition. The notes say how the conditions were compared (paired or unpaired) and which datasets were left out. For each measure, a table gives the change with its 95 % interval, p and q (corrected for the number of pairs tested), and the value of every replicate. Read q, and check whether the change goes in the same direction in every replicate. Comparing conditions explains how to label the datasets, how the test works, and how much it can detect with a few donors.

Technical: summing over datasets

interactions.tsv holds the contact table of every dataset and, for each experiment, a row "(all)". In that row, the contacts, the touching cells and the expected contacts are summed over the datasets of the experiment, and observed / expected is computed from those sums. It is not the mean of the ratios of the datasets, because that would give a small dataset as much weight as a large one.

pages.title: The output folder
pages.html:
The project folder

File Contents
project.toml the project: the exports, channel names, roles and settings (see Settings files)
overview.tsv one row per dataset of the project (the overview); result folders of datasets no longer in the project are left out
interactions.tsv the contact tables of all datasets, and their sums per experiment
membrane pairs.tsv the membrane pairs of all datasets, for every marker of interest
condition comparison.tsv the comparison of the conditions (only when every dataset has a condition and a replicate): one row per measure, pair and condition, with the change, its 95 % interval, p, q, the value per replicate, and notes; see Comparing conditions
subset preference.tsv the subset preference of all datasets (with intervals), and its sums per experiment (without intervals)
<experiment>/<dataset>/ the results of one dataset (see below)

The folder of a dataset

The tables are tab-separated text files (.tsv) with 3 decimals. NaN marks a value that does not exist, such as the mean of no values. For an IDEAS export, the tables with one row per cell or per event end with the column Object ID, which holds the IDEAS object number.

File Contents
Cell classification.tsv one row per cell: the measurements, cell type, subtype and neighbors (see below)
All cell combinations.tsv one row per event: the number of cells of each type, each marker of interest at the interfaces (its columns end in the marker's name, for example mean tumor interface (Marker); none without a marker of interest), whether a tumor cell and an immune cell touch (Tumor-immune interface), and the contacts
Single Tumor Single Immune cell.tsv the events with exactly one tumor cell and one immune cell that touch
Marker thresholds.tsv the threshold of every subtype marker, both for the artefact rule and on the immune cells, as background-subtracted intensity (on the same scale as Mean ch<N>), and how it was found (how)
Interactions.tsv the contacts per cell type and neighbor type, compared with chance
Membrane pairs.tsv for every marker of interest (column marker, and in marker on the cell type that carries it), every pair of Membrane of and Interface with: the cells with an interface, the median enrichment (median log2 ratio interface/free, and in SD median stdDevs above mean), the ratio, the scores above same-type contacts (median log2 ratio above same-type contacts, median above same-type contacts), the excess over both membranes (experimental), and the marker check (only with the membrane analysis)
Subset preference.tsv per immune subtype and partner: the contacts compared with those when the subtypes are shuffled among the immune cells of each event, with the 95 % interval (only with two or more immune subtypes)
Multiplets.tsv the number of events with n cells and with n contacts
Membrane location.tsv where the membrane lies relative to the outline: per cell type, place (free membrane or contacts with a cell type) and marker of interest, the peak of the average profile across the outline (µm, + is outside), the cells, whether it placed the band, and the spread of single cells (only with the membrane analysis)
Membrane location - profiles.tsv those average profiles across the outline, one row per distance
Membrane intensity analysis - <marker>.tsv one row per measured cell: the interface and membrane means, their ratio, the enrichment (log2 ratio interface/non-interface, and in SD stdDevs above mean), the same minus the median at same-type contacts (log2 ratio above same-type contacts, stdDevs above same-type contacts), the excess over both membranes (excess stdDevs above both membranes, experimental), and the control
Average normalized membrane profile values - interfaces centered at 20 - <marker>.tsv the average aligned profile in SD (profile), that of the excess over both membranes (excess profile), and the mean log2 ratio of every position to the free membrane (log2 ratio profile)
Histogram_interface_stdDevs_above_mean - <marker>.tsv, Histogram_control_stdDevs_above_mean - <marker>.tsv the histograms (in SD)
Control windows stdDevs above mean - <marker>.tsv every random control window, with both scores
membrane_profiles_normalized - <marker>.tif the aligned profiles, with one row for each row of the membrane table
labelmap_cells.tif, labelmap_cells.json the labels as Cellpose made them (the montage), and what produced them; the next run reuses them when nothing has changed (see Segmentation)
labelmap_final.tif, labelmap_classes.tif the cleaned-up labels per event; the cell type per pixel (1 immune, 2 tumor, 3 artefact)
dashboard.html, dashboard_files/ the dashboard
settings.toml the complete settings of the run (with channels by number)
run.json, summary.json, log.txt the version, counts, Cellpose version and device, timing, and for every marker of interest the cell type that carries it, its membrane pair and its marker check; the log

The membrane files exist only when the membrane analysis was run. The files from Membrane intensity analysis to membrane_profiles_normalized exist once for each marker of interest, with " - " and the marker's name before the extension, for example Membrane intensity analysis - Marker.tsv and membrane_profiles_normalized - Marker.tif (characters that a file name cannot hold are replaced by _). Results written before November 2026 have these names without the marker; the overview still reads such folders, but run them again to compare their membranes.

The cell table

Column Meaning
Immune intensity, Tumor intensity the mean of the normalized immune markers (summed) and of the normalized tumor marker in the cell
Marker ratio, Marker ratio over Area the immune intensity divided by the tumor intensity; the same ratio divided by the area (the k-means uses these)
Area, Area (µm²) the area in pixels; the area in square micrometers
Class, Cell type 0 tumor, 1 immune, 2 artefact; Tumor, Immune, Artefact
Frame, Label the event (1-based) and the cell's label (unique within the dataset)
Edge 1 when the cell is cut by the edge of its event image
Mean ch<N> (<name>) the mean of every loaded channel, minus the background of that channel
<marker>+ 0 or 1 for each subtype marker (using the threshold of the immune cells)
Positive markers the number of subtype markers in which the detection is positive (using the thresholds of the artefact rule)
Subtype the immune subtype (for example "A+ B+" or "negative"); empty for other cells
Neighbours, Touching (labels), Neighbour types the cells it touches: how many, which ones (by label), and their types
Object ID the IDEAS object number of the event
Technical: names that differ from the Fiji macro

Where the macro v1.8 says T cell, this program says immune cell (as ClassifyCellTypes 2.8 does), because the immune side can be defined by several markers. The macro's table Single Tumor Single T cell is therefore called Single Tumor Single Immune cell here, and its columns T-cell intensity, T cells, mean Tcell interface and T cell membrane ratio are called Immune intensity, Immune cells, mean immune interface and Immune membrane ratio. The other columns keep the macro's names, and new columns come after them.

pages.title: Input
pages.html:
IDEAS exports

The input is an export from IDEAS: a zip file with one folder per dataset. Each folder holds one image per object and channel, named <object>_Ch<N>.ome.tif. If a file-name prefix was set on export, the names read <prefix>_<object>_Ch<N>.ome.tif (the prefix is often the name of the data file); the object number is then the last number before _Ch. Every object (an ImageStream event) becomes one image in the analysis. The images are ordered by object number, and the object number is kept with every result in the Object ID column.

If one folder holds files with different prefixes, for example the exports of two data files put into the same folder, each prefix becomes a dataset of its own, named folder - prefix. Their object numbers can be the same, so they are never mixed. A small extra dataset of this kind is often a few files copied into the wrong folder: check it, and untick it on the import page if it does not belong there.

Only the channels that have been given a name are read. An object that lacks an image for one of these channels is left out, and the log reports how many objects were left out.

Which objects the export contains is decided in IDEAS, by the gates and by the population that was exported. The analysis sees no other objects. This matters when you interpret the cell contacts.

Technical: image size, background and padding

In IDEAS, the image size differs from object to object. Every image is therefore centered in an image the size of the largest one, and the border around it is filled with the channel's background. The background is computed as follows: first the median of each object's image, and then the median of those values over all objects. The same background is subtracted from the mean intensity of each cell (Mean ch<N>), and it sets the lower end of the display range in the dashboard. These are the same rules that ImageStreamCombiner (BioImaging-NKI) uses, so an export that is read directly gives the same images as a Combiner stack.

The extent of each object's own image is kept, so that cells cut by the edge of their image can be detected (see Segmentation).

ImageStreamCombiner stacks

A .tif file made by ImageStreamCombiner, with one frame per event, can also be analyzed. It is given in a settings file (input.image). The channels are then numbered by their position in the stack.

Technical: what a Combiner stack lacks

A Combiner stack orders the events in the order in which the files were listed in the zip, and it does not keep the object numbers. Its results can therefore not be traced back to IDEAS objects, and "the first N events" of a stack are different events from the first N objects of the export. The padding is recognized as the outer rows and columns that contain exactly the background value in every channel.

Channels, roles and pixel size

Every channel that the analysis needs is given a name and a role: brightfield, tumor marker, immune marker(s), subtype markers or markers of interest. See The import page for how to set them. The pixel size (in µm) is set for each export, because IDEAS files do not contain it. It is used to convert areas to µm² and positions along the membrane to µm.

The first N events

With Only the first N events, only the first N objects (by object number) of each dataset are analyzed. Use it for a quick test of the settings.

pages.title: Segmentation
pages.html:
The cells in every event are segmented with Cellpose. The resulting masks are then cleaned up, and the cells are measured.

The image for Cellpose

Cellpose does not segment each event on its own. Instead, it receives one montage of all events of a dataset, placed side by side in a grid that is roughly square. The brightfield image is not used as it is, but as its local variance: how much the brightness varies within a small circle around each pixel (radius 2 px). The variance is high at the edges and in the texture of the cells and low in the empty background, so it outlines the cells.

What the montage contains depends on the Cellpose version (the Model):

  • Cellpose 3 (cyto3, as the Fiji macro). Cellpose 3 expects at most two channels with a fixed role: one that shows the whole cell ("cytoplasm") and, optionally, one that shows the nucleus. The setting Tumor / immune markers chooses the recipe:
    • nuclear (the markers stain the nucleus or fill the cell): two channels. The brightfield variance is the cytoplasm channel; the sum of the normalized tumor and immune markers is the nucleus channel.
    • membrane (the markers stain the membrane): one channel, the sum of the normalized markers and the normalized brightfield variance.
  • Cellpose 4 (cpsam). Cellpose 4 has no cytoplasm or nucleus roles: it takes up to three channels as they are. Every segmentation channel therefore goes in on its own: the brightfield variance, the tumor marker and the immune markers (summed), each normalized. Tumor / immune markers does not matter here.

Cell diameter (px) is the typical cell diameter in pixels. Model is cyto3 (Cellpose 3), cpsam (Cellpose 4), or the path of a model of your own. A model file of your own is treated as a Cellpose 3 model, unless its file name contains cpsam.

Technical: why a montage, and why a grid

A single ImageStream event shows a few cells on an empty background. That looks quite unlike the microscopy images on which the Cellpose models were trained. When the events were segmented one by one, the masks were worse and segmentation took longer. The Fiji macro put all events in a single row. A grid of about equal height and width is about 30 % faster and gives nearly the same masks (a median IoU of about 0.97 compared with the row, on validation data). Setting Montage columns to the number of events gives the single row of the macro.

Normalization: as in the macro, each marker is divided by the median, over the events, of its Otsu threshold in each event. When there are several immune markers, each is normalized separately and the results are summed.

Sizes in pixels

All sizes are given in pixels of the export. To convert a size in µm to pixels, divide it by the pixel size (1, 0.5 or 0.33 µm at 20×, 40× or 60×).

Pixel size 15 µm cell: diameter its area 25 µm cell: diameter its area
1 µm (20×) 15 px about 180 px 25 px about 490 px
0.5 µm (40×) 30 px about 700 px 50 px about 2000 px
0.33 µm (60×) 45 px about 1600 px 75 px about 4400 px
  • Cell diameter (px): if the two cell types differ in size, start with a value between the two sizes, closer to the smaller one. Then check in the dashboard that large cells are not split and small cells are not merged. Alternatively, set it to 0 to let Cellpose 3 estimate the diameter.
  • Min. / Max. cell size (px): these are areas after shrinking. Keep the minimum well below the area of the smallest cells (about a third of it), and the maximum above the area of the largest cells.
  • Membrane / interface width (px): when left empty (the default), it is about 1.5 µm, which is 2 px at 20×, 3 px at 40× and 5 px at 60×. The same width is the distance within which two cells count as touching (see Cell contacts).

Clean-up

  1. A cell that Cellpose drew across the border between two events in the montage is split into one cell per event.
  2. Shrink cells (px): the cells are shrunk by this number of pixels where they border the background, but not where they border each other.
  3. Min. / Max. cell size (px): cells whose area after shrinking lies outside this range are removed.
Technical: details of the clean-up

Shrinking is a 4-connected binary erosion of all cells together, multiplied by the label image, as CLIJ2 does it in the macro. As a result, touching cells stay in contact, which the contacts and interfaces depend on. As in the macro, the size filter is only applied when the cells are shrunk (Shrink cells > 0). The labels are numbered 1…N in the order of the events. Each cell's label is unique within the dataset and identifies the cell in the tables.

Cells at the image edge

A cell that is cut by the edge of its event's own image (not of the padded frame) gets Edge = 1 in the cell table. Its area and outline are incomplete, and so is its membrane. Tick Leave out cells cut by the image edge to remove these cells before the classification.

Measurements

Every cell is measured in every loaded channel. For each channel, the cell table holds the mean intensity minus the channel's background (Mean ch<N>). The area of each cell is given in pixels and in µm². The normalized tumor and immune markers give Tumor intensity and Immune intensity, which are used for the classification.

Running again without Cellpose

Every run stores the Cellpose result of each dataset (labelmap_cells.tif) together with a fingerprint of what produced it (labelmap_cells.json). When a dataset is run again and the fingerprint has not changed, Cellpose is skipped, and the log says so. The clean-up, the measurements and all later steps are still done again. Changing a threshold, the membrane pair or the clean-up settings (shrinking, cell sizes) therefore does not require a new segmentation. Switch off Reuse the previous Cellpose result if nothing changed (segmentation.reuse_labels) to run Cellpose every time.

With segmentation.method = "labelmap" in a settings file, the labels of another run (labelmap_cells.tif, or the macro's labelmap_cells.zip) are loaded instead of running Cellpose.

Technical: what the fingerprint covers

The fingerprint is a hash of the image given to Cellpose and of the Cellpose settings. The image is the montage of brightfield and markers, so the hash covers the data, the channels, the number of events, the marker location and the number of montage columns. The settings are the model, the diameter, the flow and cell probability thresholds, and the Python that runs Cellpose. The GPU setting is not part of it. Results of runs made before the fingerprint was introduced have no fingerprint, so Cellpose runs once more the next time.

pages.title: Cell types
pages.html:
Every detection is classified as a tumor cell, as an immune cell with a subtype, or as an artefact. This happens in two steps. The first step decides the lineage: tumor or immune. The second step assigns a subtype to each immune cell, based on the subtype markers.

Tumor or immune cell

The cells are split into two groups by k-means clustering on three values per cell: the tumor marker and the immune marker (both normalized and on a log scale), and the area. The group with the lower ratio of immune to tumor marker is taken to be the tumor cells. This is the classification of the Fiji macro v1.8.

Technical: the clustering

The features are log(immune intensity), log(tumor intensity) and area, each scaled to a mean of 0 and an SD of 1 (using the sample SD). The k-means clustering uses 2 clusters, 10 starts and seed 48, which is the seed of the macro. The k-means of scikit-learn is not bit-identical to that of ImageJ, but on well-separated data the result is the same: the classes agreed for 100 % of the cells on the validation data. The tumor cluster is the one with the lower sum of marker ratio over area, as the macro computes it. (The comment in the macro says "average"; with clusters of unequal size, the sum and the average can give different results.)

When there are several immune markers, they are summed after normalization. The immune cells can therefore be defined by a panel of markers (for example CD3 and CD56) instead of by a single marker.

A cell whose mean tumor or immune intensity is 0 or less has no logarithm. This can happen when part of a channel of an event image is empty (all pixels 0) where the cell lies, a defect of the exported image. Such a cell gets half the lowest positive intensity of the other cells instead, so that it is clustered by its other marker, and the log names its event.

Immune subtypes

Each subtype marker gets a threshold, and an immune cell above the threshold is positive for that marker. The combination of markers for which a cell is positive is its subtype, and the subtype is named after those markers: for example Subtype A+, Subtype A+ Subtype B+, or negative when the cell is positive for none of them. The thresholds are either found automatically or set by hand, in the settings (classification.thresholds) or with the sliders in the dashboard.

The setting Threshold of the subtype markers chooses the automatic method:

  • Two populations (the default): looks for a second, positive population next to the negative cells, and puts the threshold where a cell is equally likely to belong to either population. If there is no such population (because the positive cells form a tail rather than a peak), the threshold is the upper noise limit of the negative cells. This method handles a small positive population close to a large negative one, which is the usual situation for a subtype marker.
  • MaxEntropy (as in ClassifyCellTypes 2.8): finds the split of the histogram that gives the most information on both sides.
  • MaxEntropy strict: the MaxEntropy threshold, raised where necessary so that it lies at least two robust standard deviations above the middle of the negative cells. This gives fewer false positives, at the cost of a few more missed positives.
  • Otsu: the split that best separates two populations of similar size.

For every threshold, the how column of Marker thresholds.tsv states how it was found.

Check every threshold on its histogram in the dashboard before you interpret the subtype numbers. Where the negative and positive cells form two clear peaks, the threshold belongs in the gap between them. The automatic methods can miss this gap on either side (see the technical note). If you set the threshold in the gap with the slider and apply it to the project (Apply to the project…), it is then used for every output.

Technical: the thresholds

Marker intensities are roughly log-normally distributed, so the threshold is found on

x = ln(v - min v + 1)

where v is the background-subtracted mean intensity of a cell. The threshold tx is found with ImageJ's auto-threshold on a 256-bin histogram of x (as setAutoThreshold("MaxEntropy dark") in 2.8), and then transformed back: t = etx - 1 + min v. A cell is positive when v > t. The MaxEntropy, Otsu, Yen and RenyiEntropy methods are ported from ImageJ's AutoThresholder and give the same thresholds as Fiji (checked to 10⁻¹¹).

The thresholds are computed on the immune cells only. A subtype marker may also be expressed by tumor cells. Computing its threshold on the immune cells alone prevents the tumor cells from shifting it.

The automatic thresholds can be wrong in either direction. MaxEntropy often cuts in the upper tail of the negative population, so that some negative cells are called positive. On synthetic data this typically happens to 10–20 % of them, or about ten cells per marker in a dataset of a few hundred immune cells. This creates small, spurious subtypes such as A+ C+. On other data, MaxEntropy cuts into the positive population instead: in a test at 60×, it missed a quarter of the positive cells, all of which Otsu found. MaxEntropy strict can only raise the threshold. The thresholds are listed in Marker thresholds.tsv, as background-subtracted intensities (the same scale as Mean ch<N>).

Technical: Two populations, step by step

All steps work on the log scale x defined above, with one value per cell of the population: the immune cells, or, for the artefact rule, the immune cells of the first clustering.

  1. The negative cells. A kernel density estimate of x is computed (Gaussian kernel; bandwidth 0.9 · min(s, mathrmIQR/1.34) · n-1/5 by Silverman's rule; evaluated at 1024 points). Its highest peak is taken as the mode m of the negative cells. Their spread is estimated from the lower side of the peak only, which positive cells do not reach: sigma = 1.4826 · mathrmmedian(m - x) over the cells with x le m. For a normal distribution, this equals the standard deviation. The noise limit is m + 2.5 sigma.
  2. A second population. A mixture of two normal distributions is fitted to x by expectation–maximization, starting from the mode and from the largest value, so that the result is deterministic. The upper component counts as a positive population when it contains at least 0.5 % of the cells, when its mean lies at least two pooled standard deviations from the mean of the lower component (Ashman's D ≥ 2), and when its mean lies above the noise limit.
  3. The threshold. If there is a positive population, the threshold is where the two weighted normal densities cross, between their means: above this point, a cell is more likely to be positive than negative. The threshold is never lower than m + 2sigma. If there is no positive population, the threshold is the noise limit. With fewer than ten cells, MaxEntropy is used instead.

The how column of Marker thresholds.tsv reports which case applied, together with the fraction of cells in the fitted positive population: two populations (12 % positive): crossing, ... raised to mode + 2 SD, or no second population: noise limit.

Why this method. A threshold that maximizes a criterion over the whole histogram (Otsu, MaxEntropy) is pulled into the large negative population when the positive population is small, which is the common situation for a subtype marker. A fixed distance above the negative cells (as in "strict") is right when there is no clear second population, but it cuts into a positive population that lies close to the negative one. The two steps cover both situations. The method was chosen on simulated data: 600 cells, with log-normal negative cells with noise (two spreads), positive cells making up 2–40 % of the cells and 3–40 times as bright, and five repeats (500 samples in all). The total number of errors (false plus missed positives), compared with the best possible threshold for each sample, was: best possible 2417, Two populations 4790, the noise limit alone 6825, MaxEntropy strict 14 881, Otsu 21 132 and MaxEntropy 21 965. Almost all remaining errors occur in samples where the two populations overlap (positive cells 2–5 % of the cells and at most 5 times as bright), where no threshold can separate them. On the four user-test datasets (2289 positive cells in all), Two populations made 4 errors and MaxEntropy 286.

Limits. When the positive cells form a continuous tail, the noise limit decides, and the number of positive cells depends on the choice of 2.5 SD. Set the threshold by hand if the histogram shows a better place for it. A bimodal negative population (for example, two batches of differently stained cells pooled together) can be mistaken for two populations. Classify such datasets separately (Classify together = dataset).

Technical: why two steps, and not one clustering of all cells

A single k-means clustering of all cells into k types was considered and not used, for three reasons. k-means favors groups of similar size and spread, so a small subtype is absorbed by a large neighboring group. The number k must be chosen in advance. And the clusters have to be named afterwards. A threshold per marker, in contrast, can be read, checked on its histogram and changed, and the combinations of positive markers name the subtypes directly.

Artefacts

A detection that is positive for all subtype markers (when there are two or more of them) is not taken to be a cell, but an artefact: for example debris, or a dead cell that takes up every dye. Artefacts are left out of the tumor/immune clustering and drawn in gray. They are not counted as cells, neither in the cell counts nor in the interfaces. Use Artefact: positive in at least N subtype markers to set a different number; 0 switches the rule off.

The images cannot distinguish an artefact from a real cell that is positive for every marker. If you expect such cells, look at the artefacts in the dashboard (they are drawn in gray) before you switch the rule off. With the rule off, real artefacts appear as a subtype that is positive for every marker; they are counted, and they take part in the contacts as if they were cells. With one subtype marker, the rule is off and an artefact counts as a positive immune cell (the log says so). In that case, check the positive cells by eye.

Technical: the artefact rule

The rule needs the subtype thresholds of the immune cells. These are only known after the tumor/immune clustering, but that clustering should run without the artefacts. The clustering therefore runs twice:

  1. A first k-means clustering of all detections finds the immune cells.
  2. Every subtype marker is thresholded on those immune cells, with the threshold method of the project or with the threshold set by hand. A detection that is positive for at least N markers by these thresholds is an artefact. The column Positive markers in the cell table holds the number of positive markers, and the rows "artefact rule" in Marker thresholds.tsv hold these thresholds.
  3. The final k-means clustering runs on the remaining detections. The subtype thresholds are then computed again on its immune cells (the rows "immune cells"), and may differ slightly.

Until November 2026, the thresholds of the rule were computed over all detections. For well-separated markers, these thresholds lay at the noise level of the many negative cells (including the tumor cells). A cell positive for one marker that touched a cell positive for another marker picked up a little of its neighbor's light, and so became an artefact. In a test with three subtype markers, 5 of 47 "artefacts" were such cells. With the thresholds of the immune cells, the rule found exactly the 42 artefacts that had been simulated.

Only the subtype markers count. Counting the tumor and immune markers as well (a detection that is bright for both could be two cells drawn as one) was tried and dropped. An automatic threshold of those markers over all detections calls far more cells positive than the clustering finds, so most detections would become artefacts.

Several datasets: pools

With Classify together = experiment (the default), the cells of all datasets with the same experiment label are classified together, with one clustering and one set of thresholds. A cell that is "Subtype A+" is then positive by the same standard in every dataset of the experiment, so the subtype fractions can be compared between datasets. With dataset, each dataset gets its own thresholds.

Technical: when to pool

Pool datasets that were stained and acquired in the same way (an experiment). Each dataset keeps its own background and its own normalization of the tumor and immune markers; only the clustering and the thresholds are shared. Datasets from different staining batches or with different instrument settings can differ in brightness. Give them different experiment labels, or classify each dataset separately. With pooling, the run first measures all datasets, then classifies each experiment, and then finishes each dataset. run.json records what each dataset was classified with.

Colors

The dashboard gives up to eight cell types their own color (tumor, up to six immune types, and artefacts), in a fixed order, so that a cell type keeps its color when other types appear or disappear. Any further immune types share a gray color. The legends and tables always name the cell types.

pages.title: Cell contacts
pages.html:
Which cells touch

Two cells in the same event touch when one of them lies within Membrane / interface width of the other. If this setting is left empty (the default), the width is about 1.5 µm, which is 2 px at 20×, 3 px at 40× and 5 px at 60×. This is the same distance that defines the interfaces, so a cell with an interface always lists its partner among the cells it touches. Cells in different events never touch.

For every cell, the column Touching (labels) lists the cells it touches, and Neighbour types lists their cell types. For every event, the column Interactions gives the number of touching pairs.

Technical: the distance

"Within k pixels" means within k steps between 4-connected pixels. This is the reach of the dilation that makes the interfaces (done with CLIJ2 in the macro). Two cells with no background pixel between them are 1 step apart; two cells with a gap of g pixels between them are g + 1 steps apart. ClassifyCellTypes 2.8 used the region adjacency graph of MorphoLibJ on the shrunk labels, which counts only cells that touch directly. Here, cells that almost touch also count, as they do for the interfaces.

The default is set in µm rather than in pixels, so that "touching" means the same at every magnification. The width in pixels is the whole number nearest to 1.5 mumathrmm / pixel size, with a minimum of 2. A fixed width of 3 px would mean 3 µm at 20× (so that near misses would count as contacts) and 1 µm at 60×. If you set the width in pixels, that value is used as it is.

Counting contacts

Interactions.tsv and the dashboard give, for each cell type (row) and each cell type it touches (column):

  • contacts: the number of touching pairs. A pair of an A cell and a B cell counts once in row A and once in row B.
  • cells touching: the number of cells of the row's type that touch at least one cell of the column's type, and the fraction of the row's cells that this represents.

Partner preference: contacts compared with chance

The plain counts mostly reflect how many cells of each type there are. To see whether some cell types prefer each other, the observed contacts are compared with chance. The expected number of contacts is the number you would get if the cell types were shuffled among the cells of each event, while the cells in every event and the number of contacts in it stay as they are. The ratio observed / expected is above 1 when two cell types touch more often than random pairing of the cells within their events would give, and below 1 when they touch less often.

Only events with three or more cells are used. In an event of two touching cells, the pair can only be the pair it is, so observed and expected are equal by construction, whatever the biology. Such events would pull every ratio towards 1. They are therefore left out of this comparison, although they still count in the plain contacts. The dashboard shows how many pairs remain.

Technical: the expected contacts, exactly

No random shuffling is done: the expected number is computed exactly. Take an event of n cells, of which cA are of type A. A given touching pair in that event consists of an A cell and a B cell (A ≠ B) with probability

pAB = (2 cA cB) / (n (n-1))

and of two A cells with probability cA (cA - 1) / (n (n-1)). The expected number of contacts of A with B is the sum, over all events of three or more cells, of (number of pairs in the event) × pAB. It is counted from both sides, in the same way as the observed contacts (so an A–A pair counts twice). As a result, the page and Interactions.tsv give identical numbers. Pairs of cell types that never touch, but would touch by chance, also get a row, with 0 observed contacts: this indicates avoidance.

The total of the expected contacts equals the total of the observed contacts: chance only redistributes the contacts over the cell types.

What the selection in IDEAS means

The export contains only the objects that were selected in IDEAS. Often these are only multiplets, without single cells, and sometimes only events that contain both cell types. The comparison with chance takes into account which cells are in each event, because it shuffles only within an event. It does not take into account why an event was exported. The question it answers is therefore:

Within the exported multiplets of three or more cells, which cell types touch each other more, or less, than random pairing of the cells in their events would give?

It does not answer how often immune cells bind tumor cells in the sample. That would need the cells that never touched another cell (the singlets) and the events without contacts, and these are not in the export. A conjugate frequency (for example "the percentage of T cells in conjugates") can only be computed from an export that keeps all events, including the singlets.

Technical: further limits of the null model
  • The model assumes that every pair of cells in an event is equally likely to touch. In reality, a large cell has more room for neighbors than a small one. In an event with one large cell and several small ones, the large cell therefore takes part in more contacts than chance predicts. Comparing the same cell types between conditions is safer than interpreting a single ratio on its own.
  • Small numbers give large ratios. A ratio of 2 based on 2 observed contacts and 1 expected contact means little. The tooltip in the dashboard and the table both give the counts, so check them.
  • Artefacts take part in the comparison like any other cell type. With a stricter artefact rule, cells move from the artefacts to the cell types, and the other way round with a looser rule.
  • In tests without any preference, tumor–tumor came out at about 1.5, because larger cells have more neighbors. Real preferences, on the other hand, come out weaker than they are. In one test, a subset that was placed next to tumor cells far more often after a treatment rose only from 1.03 to 1.11, although it did so consistently in both donors. So compare datasets (donors, conditions) with each other, rather than comparing a single ratio with 1.

Subset preference: which immune cells touch

The partner preference above shuffles all cell types. It therefore compares tumor cells with immune cells, which differ in size. For the immune subtypes, a cleaner question can be asked: when an event offers a choice of immune cells, is the immune cell that touches the tumor cell (or another immune cell) of this subtype more often than chance would predict? To answer this, only the subtypes are shuffled, among the immune cells of each event. The cells, their positions, the tumor cells and the contacts all stay as they are. Only events with at least two immune cells are used, because with a single immune cell there is no choice.

The result is the ratio observed / expected for each subtype and each partner (tumor cells or an immune subtype), with a 95 % interval. No interval is given when fewer than 5 contacts are expected. In the dashboard (Interactions, tab among immune cells), only the squares whose interval excludes 1 are colored. Because many squares are tested at once, about one square in twenty will exclude 1 by chance alone. Trust a preference that is found in every dataset (donor, replicate), not a single square. The results are in Subset preference.tsv for each dataset and in subset preference.tsv in the project folder.

Technical: the subset preference, exactly

Expected. Take an event with n immune cells, of which cS are of subtype S. When the subtypes are shuffled among these cells, every immune cell has subtype S with probability cS / n. Each immune–tumor contact in the event therefore involves a cell of subtype S with that probability. Each immune–immune contact involves subtypes S and T with probability 2 cS cT / (n (n − 1)), or two cells of subtype S with probability cS (cS − 1) / (n (n − 1)); these are counted from both sides, as in the contact table. The expected number of contacts is the sum of these probabilities over the contacts of all events with n ≥ 2. The observed number is the number of contacts counted in the same events (contacts). Artefacts are not included, and tumor cells are never shuffled.

The interval. The events are resampled with replacement (as many events as there are), observed and expected are summed again, and the ratio observed / expected is recomputed. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of this ratio over the resamples form the interval. Python uses 1000 resamples with a fixed seed, so that the tables are reproducible; the page uses 400, so its interval is slightly different. The interval reflects the sampling of events within one dataset, not the variation between donors; compare datasets for that. Below 5 expected contacts no interval is given. A resample of only a handful of contacts often contains the same contacts every time, which gives an interval of zero width that excludes 1 on the basis of one or two contacts.

Why within events. Shuffling the subtypes over the whole dataset asks whether a subtype is over-represented among the immune cells that touch tumor cells. In an export of conjugates, nearly every immune cell touches a tumor cell (95 % in the example data), so that ratio can hardly exceed about 1.05, whatever the biology. Within an event that offers a choice, it can. In the example data, cells of Subtype A+ were placed next to the tumor cell more often. The dataset-wide version gave 1.00 (0.93–1.08), and the within-event version 1.09 (1.03–1.17). The effects are small in both versions because most events offer little choice: when an event has one tumor cell and two immune cells, both immune cells usually touch it.

What it does not correct for. A subtype that is larger, or that is more often segmented as two cells, still touches more often. The subtypes are assumed to be of similar size. The limits of the selection in IDEAS, described above, apply here too.

Comparing conditions

The experiment label does two things. Datasets with the same label are classified together, with one threshold per marker (see pools), and the overview adds them up into one partner-preference matrix. To compare, for example, control and treated samples that were stained in the same way:

  • Give them one experiment label, so that "positive for A" means the same in both (or set the thresholds by hand).
  • Give every dataset its condition and its replicate (donor). The overview then tests the change in subset preference across the donors, with an interval and a correction for the number of pairs tested; see Comparing conditions. The overview's matrix for each experiment pools the conditions, so it cannot show a change.
  • Expect small numbers. Few events give the immune cells a choice, so real changes in preference come out weak. In a test where a subset was placed next to the tumor cell more than twice as often after treatment, the ratio rose by 0.05–0.25. In a simulation with the event geometry of real data, it rose by about as much: the tool cannot recover more than the events contain. How many donors and events are needed to detect such a change is described in Comparing conditions.

Multiplets

Multiplets.tsv counts the events with n cells and the events with n contacts (n = 0, 1, 2, …), like the multiplets table of ClassifyCellTypes 2.8.

pages.title: Membrane enrichment
pages.html:
This analysis asks a simple question: is there more of a marker in a cell's membrane where it touches another cell than in the rest of its membrane? For example: does a ligand on tumor cells gather where a T cell touches? Tick Membrane profiles and enrichment to switch it on. With several markers of interest, every marker is analyzed in the same way (see Several markers of interest).

The answer is less simple than the question. Images of touching cells contain several effects that look like enrichment but are not: two stained membranes lying side by side, a partner that carries the marker too, and an outline that does not lie exactly on the membrane. This page explains each step, what can go wrong, and what the program does about it. The main text is meant to be read from top to bottom; the folded Technical notes give the details for those who want them.

In short, for every cell the program:

  1. traces the cell's outline and finds where the stained membrane lies relative to that outline;
  2. reads the marker along the membrane, as a line of values from one end of the membrane to the other (the membrane profile);
  3. notes, for every point of that line, whether another cell touches there, and which one;
  4. compares the part that touches a partner (the interface) with the part that touches no cell at all (the free membrane).

The result is a score per cell, and a median per pair of cell types. Random stretches of free membrane serve as a control, and contacts between cells of the same kind serve as a reference for what touching alone does.

The membrane profile

Imagine laying a ribbon along the edge of the cell, and reading the marker under the ribbon at every step along the edge. That is what the program does: it traces the cell's outline, smooths it, and takes a band of pixels across the membrane at every point along it. Laid out straight, the band becomes a strip; this is called straightening. At every point along the membrane, the brightest pixel across the band is kept. The result is the membrane profile: one value per pixel of perimeter, with the background subtracted.

The width of the band is Straightening width. By default it is about 4.5 µm (5 px at 20×, 9 px at 40×, 13 px at 60×). It has to be wide enough to contain the membrane everywhere, also where the outline does not lie exactly on it (see the next section).
