Along the same line, the program also records, for every point, whether another cell lies within Membrane / interface width (by default about 1.5 µm), and if so which cell. This record is the cell's neighbor track. It decides which points are interface and which are free membrane.

Technical: one membrane per cell, and how the outline is traced

The Fiji macro straightened one ring for each blob of touching cells of the same type. Here every cell has its own membrane, so two touching tumor cells give two membranes. The outline follows the pixel edges of the cell's mask (marching squares) and is smoothed with a Gaussian (σ = 2 samples), where Fiji fits a spline; it is then resampled at 1 px, so a profile has one value per pixel of perimeter. For the neighbor track, every pixel of the cell that lies within the interface width of another cell gets the label of the nearest other cell; the track is read along the outline. The length of every profile is stored, so a value of 0 is data and does not mark the end of the profile (in the macro, zeros ended it).

Where the band is placed

The problem: the outline is not the membrane

The outline comes from the cell's mask, which Cellpose draws. It is close to the membrane, but not on it, and how far off it is depends on where you look:

  • Where a cell is free, the mask usually reaches a little beyond the stained membrane, because the blurred edge of the cell is included. The membrane then lies a little inside the outline, typically less than a micrometre (about 1 µm in the synthetic tests).
  • Where two cells touch, the outline is the border between the two masks. Cellpose has to put that border somewhere in the blurred contact, and it need not be exactly on the membrane either. On real data, it sometimes lay a little into one of the two cells.

So the distance between outline and membrane differs between the free membrane and the interface, and between cell types. If the band is centred on the outline, it can reach more of the membrane at the interface than at the free membrane. The interface then looks brighter than the free membrane even if the marker is spread evenly. This is a false enrichment: it comes from the geometry, not from the biology.

What the program does: find the membrane first

Before it measures anything, the program finds out where the membrane really lies. For each cell type, it averages the marker across the outline (3 µm to each side) over all its cells: once along the free membrane, and once along the contacts with each other cell type. The peak of each average is where the membrane lies. The band is then centred on that peak: at the free membrane on the free peak, at a contact on the peak for that kind of contact. Where a contact begins or ends, the band moves over smoothly.

You can see the result in the dashboard: the membrane card has a folded section Across the membrane, which shows these averages and where the band lies; and in the Cell card, membrane band (or the space bar) draws the band of a cell over its images.

Band centred on has three choices:

Choice The band lies Use it
membrane (default) where the membrane lies, for each cell type (one place for all cells of a type, at the free membrane and at each kind of contact) in general
cell as membrane, but each cell's free membrane on its own peak when the cells differ a lot in how far the outline lies from the membrane
outline on the outline, as the Fiji macro did to compare with the macro, or to see how much the placement matters

The Straightening width still matters, but much less. Centring removes the systematic difference between free membrane and interface; the width takes up what remains (cells differ from each other). Keep the default width unless you have a reason to change it.

Technical: how the membrane is found

For every measured cell, every marker of interest is sampled along lines perpendicular to the outline, from 3 µm inside to 3 µm outside, in steps of a quarter pixel. These samples are averaged along the points of the cell that are free membrane (if there are at least 5), and separately along the points that touch each cell type. The cell averages are then averaged over all cells of the same type. The peak of such an average (refined with a parabola through the three highest points) is the distance from the outline to the membrane for that cell type and place. A peak at the very end of the 3 µm window is not accepted.

Which marker places the band. The membrane of a cell type is located with a marker of interest that this cell type carries: its free membrane must be at least half as bright as that of the brightest cell type (measured on the same averages). A marker that a cell type does not carry shows no membrane of that cell, or signal somewhere else in it (on real data, one marker showed a sharp peak well inside the other cell type, probably signal inside the cell). With several markers carried by the same type, the marker most specific to that type is used, and if two are equally specific, the one with the clearest peak. Its place then holds for all markers, because the membrane is where it is, whatever the marker.

When the band stays on the outline. If no marker of interest is carried by a cell type, if fewer than 20 cells contribute to an average, or if the average has no clear peak (its peak must stand out by at least 30 % of its range above the ends of the window), the band stays on the outline there. The log says so for every cell type and place.

The neighbor track is always read along the outline itself, so moving the band does not change which points are interface and which are free membrane.

Technical: cell — a place per cell, and why not at the contacts

With cell, every cell's free membrane is placed on the peak of its own average (from the same marker as its type), and its contacts are moved by the same amount, plus its type's difference between contact and free membrane. Example: if tumor cells have their free membrane on average 0.9 µm inside the outline and their contacts with immune cells 0.3 µm outside it, a tumor cell whose own free membrane lies 1.2 µm inside gets its contacts with immune cells at 0.0 µm.

Contacts are never placed per cell, for two reasons. They are short, so the peak of a single contact is noisy. And letting the marker choose where to sample exactly the place that is tested would push the interface up: the brightest spot nearby always looks a little enriched. Cells with fewer than 20 points of free membrane, or without a clear peak of their own, use the type's place. The log says how many cells had a place of their own.

Is the per-cell place real, or noise? On real datasets, the place found on one half of a cell's free membrane agreed well with the place found on the other half, and cells differed from each other by about as much as the type's average distance. cell follows that variation.

Technical: what was seen on real data

On real data, the free membrane of both cell types lay on average somewhat inside the outline (less than a micrometre), and single cells varied around that by about as much. At contacts, the two cell types differed. For one type, the membrane lay just as far inside the outline at contacts as at the free membrane, so a band on the outline treated both alike. For the other type, the membrane at contacts lay on or slightly beyond the outline, while the free membrane lay inside it. A band on the outline then reached the two places differently, and how that shifted the score depended on the band width: with a narrow band it could raise the score of some pairs and lower that of others. Centring the band on the membrane made the scores depend much less on the width.

Contacts between cells of the same type, where no enrichment is expected, came out lower once the band was centred, which is what removing a false enrichment should do.

Technical: the straightening width with the band on the outline

In a synthetic test at 40× (0.5 µm per pixel), with the band on the outline, a ligand on the tumor membrane was enriched only where Beta+ immune cells touched. The tumor cells' interface with Beta− cells, which has no enrichment, measured:

Straightening width Beta− contacts (truth: none) Beta+ contacts (truth: enriched)
5 px (2.5 µm; the macro's value) 1.4–1.6 SD, ratio 1.31 7.2–7.5 SD, ratio 2.5–2.65
9 px (4.5 µm) 0.35 SD, ratio 1.05 6.5–6.7 SD, ratio 1.95–2.0
13 px (6.5 µm) 0.2 SD, ratio 1.03 6.6–7.1 SD, ratio 1.9

This is why the default width is about 4.5 µm: the odd number of pixels nearest to 4.5 µm divided by the pixel size, with a minimum of 5. A wider band somewhat lowers the ratio of a real enrichment, because the free membrane is now measured at its true brightness, but the real enrichment stays clearly apart from the false one. If you set the width in pixels (membrane.straightening_width), that value is used as it is. The comparison with the Fiji macro uses the macro's 5 px with the band on the outline.

With the band centred on the membrane, the width matters much less: in a synthetic test with an evenly stained membrane that lay 2 px inside a free outline, a 3 px band on the outline made the interface look about 30 % brighter than the free membrane; centred on the membrane, a 3 px and a 9 px band both showed no enrichment.

A wider band also reaches further into a touching partner. This matters when the partner carries the marker (see Where the marker is expressed).

A pair of cell types

Membrane of and Interface with choose the pair of cell types: whose membrane is measured, and which partners make up the interface. Each can be:

  • a cell type (Tumor, Immune);
  • an immune subtype as it is named in the tables (Immune Subtype A+, or Immune negative for the immune cells that are negative for every subtype marker);
  • a marker (Subtype A+: every immune cell that is positive for that marker, whatever its other markers).

Anything else (for example Immune Subtype A without the +) stops the run before it starts, with a message that suggests what was probably meant.

If Membrane of is left empty, the program measures the cell type that carries the marker: the tumor cells or the immune cells, whichever has the brighter membrane. This is decided from the data, for each marker of interest separately. If Interface with is left empty, the partners are the other cell type. Every marker of interest has a pair of its own, and each side is set on its own. In the dashboard you can change the pair directly.

The log says which cell type carries each marker, and how clearly. In the example (Donor 1): "Marker: carried by the tumor cells (...): membranes of Tumor with Immune". The same is recorded in run.json (markers of interest), in the column marker on of Membrane pairs.tsv, and in the overview column MOI on of each marker. If the two cell types carry the marker at a similar level (the weaker one at 80 % of the stronger or more), the choice is made by a small margin, and the log warns. Then set the pair yourself, so that it does not depend on that margin.

Technical: how the carrying cell type is decided

With the membrane analysis, the measure is the height of the free membrane in the marker averaged across the outline (the same averages that place the band): the peak of that average above its ends, for the tumor cells and for the immune cells. The type with the higher peak carries the marker. This measure does not depend on the band's width or place. (Until November 2026 the band's own free-membrane values were used; when a marker was on both cell types at a similar level, the choice could then flip when only the band width changed.) Without the membrane analysis, the median whole-cell intensity is used instead.

Before November 2026, the measured type was a setting (Marker of interest expressed in). A settings file or project that still has it (channels.cell_of_interest) loads without an error; the setting is ignored, and the log says so.

For the measured cells, the interface is the part of the membrane where the neighbor track shows a partner. The free membrane is the part that touches no cell at all. Contacts with cells that are not partners belong to neither: they are left out of the comparison.

The score

For every measured cell that has an interface, the analysis compares the mean of the profile at the interface with the mean of the free membrane (both after the background is subtracted). The main score is the log2 ratio:

log2 ratio = log2 (interface) / (free)

It reads as a fold change: 0 means the interface is as bright as the free membrane, 1 twice as bright, 2 four times, and −1 half as bright. A log2 ratio of 0.5 is about 40 % more marker at the contact.

The tables also keep the macro's score, SD above mean: how far the interface lies above the free membrane, in standard deviations of the free membrane:

SD above mean = (interface - free) / (SD(free))

The profiles are aligned so that the center of the longest interface of each cell lies at the same place: position 20 in the output files, 0 µm in the dashboard. Their average, over the cells with an interface, shows the shape of the enrichment.

Technical: why the log2 ratio, and not SD above mean

Both scores compare the interface with the cell's own free membrane. They differ in what they divide by: the ratio divides by the mean of the free membrane, the SD score by its spread.

  • The spread mixes in other things. The standard deviation of the free membrane grows with patchy staining (clusters, microvilli), with noise, and with where the band lies. A cell with an evenly stained membrane gets a large SD score for a small enrichment; a patchy cell gets a small score for a large one. If a treatment makes the marker more clustered without bringing more of it to the contact, the SD score changes and the ratio does not.
  • Brightness. Dim cells are relatively noisier, so their SD scores shrink, and bright cells get large ones. The ratio does not depend on how much marker a cell carries.
  • Stability. A mean from a short free membrane is estimated much better than a standard deviation, so the ratio has fewer extreme values.
  • Statistics. log2 ratios are symmetric (twice as bright = +1, half = −1) and close to a normal distribution, which suits the tests of the comparison of conditions.
  • Meaning. "1.4 times as bright" can be judged biologically and compared with other studies; "2 SD" depends on the cell.

Its weak point is the background. A ratio needs a correct zero: an offset that is subtracted too little or too much biases it, while the SD score does not care. And a cell whose free membrane is about as dark as the background has no meaningful ratio: the program leaves the log2 ratio empty when either mean is 0 or below. So the log2 ratio is reliable for the cell type that carries the marker, and much less so for a type that hardly carries it (the marker check marks such pairs with "–"). The SD score does say whether the interface stands out from the cell's own fluctuations; the control windows answer that for both scores.

Technical: why the free membrane is the baseline

The macro compared the interface with the rest of the membrane, including the parts that touch other cells. A contact with another cell that carries the marker (for example between two tumor cells, when the marker is on tumor cells) places two membranes side by side and is therefore brighter. It would raise the baseline and lower the enrichment. Here the baseline is the membrane that touches no cell. On validation data, this raised the median enrichment by about 0.2 SD, while the control stayed the same.

Ways to score an interface

The dashboard's Measure menu offers five scores. The tables of the output folder contain all of them.

Measure What it compares When to use it
log2 ratio to own membrane (default) the interface with the cell's own free membrane, as a fold change when the partners carry little or none of the marker (the marker check is green)
log2 ratio above same-type contacts the same, minus the median log2 ratio of the measured cells at contacts with cells of their own kind when the partners carry the marker too: it asks whether the contact with this partner is brighter than a contact between two cells of the measured kind
SD above own membrane as the first, in standard deviations of the free membrane (the macro's score) to compare with results of the Fiji macro
SD above same-type contacts as the second, in standard deviations as above
SD above both membranes (experimental) the interface with the own free membrane plus the partner's free membrane to explore; read the note below before relying on it

Why the same-type versions? At an interface, the membranes of the two cells lie so close together that the microscope cannot separate them. If the partner carries the marker too, the interface contains two stained membranes, and it looks brighter even without any enrichment. A score against the own membrane cannot tell this apart from a real enrichment.

The same-type versions use the data themselves as the reference. A contact between two tumor cells also places two stained membranes side by side, with the same kind of geometry, but with no partner-specific biology. If a tumor–immune contact scores higher than a tumor–tumor contact, that difference is what the immune partner adds. A score of 0 means "as bright as a contact between two cells of the measured kind"; in log2, a value of 0.5 means 40 % brighter than such a contact.

Technical: the scores above same-type contacts, exactly

For the measured cells of a pair (Membrane of), the program takes the score of each of them at its contacts with cells of the same selection: tumor cells with tumor cells, Immune Subtype A+ cells with Immune Subtype A+ cells, and so on. The median of these scores is the reference; it needs at least 10 cells with such a contact (otherwise the measure is empty). Each cell's score minus the reference is its score above same-type contacts. In log2 this is a ratio of ratios: how much brighter the contact with the partner is than a same-type contact. In the files: the columns log2 ratio above same-type contacts and stdDevs above same-type contacts of Membrane intensity analysis - <marker>.tsv, and median log2 ratio above same-type contacts and median above same-type contacts in Membrane pairs.tsv. In the dashboard, the histograms, the heatmap order, the All pairs table, the cell card and the Cells table follow the measure; the average profile stays that of the own membrane, with a dashed line at the reference.

When it is not a fair reference. It assumes that a contact with the partner is, apart from the biology, like a contact between two measured cells. That holds best when the partner carries about as much of the marker as the measured cells (the marker check says on both cells). If the partner carries much less, the same-type contacts contain more marker than a fair reference would, and the measure is too strict: it can hide an enrichment. If the partner carries more, the reference is too lenient. Cells of different sizes also touch in different ways. Read it together with the marker check, and with SD above own membrane.

Technical: SD above both membranes (experimental), and why it fails its own check

The idea: if the intensities of two touching membranes simply add, the partner's share can be subtracted. For every measured cell with an interface:

excess = (interface - free - partner free) / (SD(free))

Here partner free is, at every interface point, the mean free-membrane intensity of the partner cell that touches there, averaged over the interface. A partner without any free membrane is left out; if no partner of the cell has a free membrane, the excess is empty. The control windows have no partner, so their excess is the control itself. Files: the column excess stdDevs above both membranes of the membrane table, excess profile in the average profile, and median excess above both membranes in Membrane pairs.tsv.

The check it fails. For contacts between cells of the same type, where both carry the marker and nothing is expected, the excess should be about 0. On real data it was clearly negative for every band placement (outline, per type, per cell), every width tried (3, 5 and 9 px) and both ways of reading across the band (maximum and sum): the subtraction takes away more than the partner adds. Centring the band on the membrane even made it more negative, because the free membrane is then measured at its peak. So it is not a matter of where the band lies. Likely reasons, not proven: the images are 2D projections of 3D cells, so a contact that is tilted is not seen as two membranes side by side, and cells that overlap in depth blur differently than free membranes; and a membrane may carry less marker per area where it is pressed against another cell.

How to read it, if at all. A positive excess means more marker at the contact than both membranes carry elsewhere, whichever cell holds it. Because it tends to be too low, a negative value is not evidence of depletion. Check the same-type contacts of your own data in the All pairs table first. The comparison of conditions uses the log2 ratio to the own membrane.

Technical: across the band — maximum or sum

The dashboard's switch across the band chooses how the band becomes one value per point. maximum (the default, as the macro and the tables) keeps the brightest pixel across the band. sum adds all pixels across the band. At an interface both membranes lie in the band; only the sum adds them up, which is what SD above both membranes assumes. The sum also counts the inside of the cell within the band, so it depends more on the band width. Everything in the membrane card follows the switch; the tables of the output folder keep the maximum.

The control

Cells without an interface get control windows: Control windows per cell (default 10) windows at random places on their free membrane. Each window is as long as the median interface and is scored like an interface, with both scores. The histogram of the controls shows how much a stretch of free membrane varies by chance in this dataset; its log2 ratio lies around 0.

In the dashboard, both histograms share one scale. For the log2 ratio it starts at −2 (one quarter) and reaches at least 2 (four times). For the SD scores it starts at −5 SD, as in the files Histogram_interface_stdDevs_above_mean - <marker>.tsv and Histogram_control_stdDevs_above_mean - <marker>.tsv (which stay in SD, as the macro's). If Histogram maximum and Histogram bin width are left empty, the scale is automatic. The maximum is the 99th percentile of the interface values or of the control windows, whichever is higher, but at least 5 SD (2 in log2), and it is rounded up to a whole number of bins. The bin width is the smallest of 0.1, 0.2, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10, and so on, that gives at most 60 bins. Values above the maximum are not counted. The two settings apply to the SD scale; you can change either scale in the dashboard without running the analysis again.

The control windows are not a control for the interface itself. Because they lie on free membrane, they cannot show what touching does to the measurement apart from the marker: two stained membranes side by side, a partner's signal blurring into the interface, and the outline lying differently at a contact. Therefore:

  • Compare pairs, not an interface with the control windows. Compare the same measured cells with partners that do carry a receptor or ligand and with partners that do not (for example Immune A+ against Immune negative). Or compare with contacts between cells of the measured kind (log2 ratio above same-type contacts, or set Interface with to the measured type itself). The dashboard shows all pairs at once (All pairs in the membrane card). In the example below, the tumor cells' membrane is enriched mainly at contacts with Subtype A+ cells.

  • A small shift (a ratio below about 1.5, a log2 ratio below about 0.6, or 1–2 SD) is within what the effects above can produce; a large effect that is specific to one pair is not.

  • Check in the dashboard that the band lies on the membrane (Cell card, membrane band; membrane card, Across the membrane).
  • A p-value from thousands of cells against thousands of windows says nothing about biological replicates. Compare datasets (donors, replicates) instead. A change between conditions is tested across the donors in the overview; see Comparing conditions.
Technical: comparing pairs, and why there is no reference channel

The pair table. For every selection under Membrane of (rows) and every cell type or subtype under Interface with (columns), the dashboard computes the median score of the measured cells that have an interface with that partner, and the number of such cells. The median is computed exactly as for the chosen pair, but without the control windows. A pair in which the measured cells or the partners do not carry the marker is the geometry-matched control for a pair in which they do: the same cells, the same kind of contact and the same segmentation. Contacts between cells of the same type show what two stained membranes side by side produce. Each entry carries the marker check of its pair: "!" when the partners carry part of the marker or as much as the measured cells, "!!" when they carry more, and "–" when the measured cells hardly carry it.

No reference channel. A second channel, measured like the marker of interest but not expected to be enriched, seemed a natural control. The cells' own tracker dye was tested as such a reference. Because the dye fills the cell, it fills the band at a contact but not at the free edge, and it showed 4.8 SD (at 5 px) and 2.7 SD (at 9 px) of "enrichment". A reference must be stained in the same way as the marker (a membrane stain on the same cells), which a panel rarely includes. The pair comparison needs no extra channel.

Technical: the control windows

The windows are drawn on the free membrane only, which is read as one closed line, and each window is scored against the rest of that free membrane. The macro used one window of 25 px per membrane; many windows of the typical interface length give a better estimate of the null distribution. The windows are random and not seeded, so the control differs slightly from run to run (the dashboard uses a fixed seed). All windows are listed in Control windows stdDevs above mean - <marker>.tsv, with both scores.

Where the marker is expressed

The marker of interest should be on the measured cells, not on their partners. At an interface, the membranes of the two cells lie against each other. If the partner also carries the marker, its membrane is measured together with that of the measured cell, and the interface looks enriched even when both cells are stained evenly.

The analysis checks this. It compares the median free-membrane intensity of the partners with that of the measured cells. The result is reported in the log, in run.json, in the overview (MOI partners / measured) and as a badge in the dashboard:

Partners / measured Badge Meaning
below 25 % ✓ green The marker is mainly on the measured cells.
25–80 % ! amber The partners carry part of the marker, so part of the interface signal may come from them.
80–125 % ! amber The marker is on both cell types at a similar level. Two stained membranes side by side look like enrichment; use log2 ratio above same-type contacts, or compare with contacts between cells of the same type.
125 % or more ! red The marker is brighter on the partners. Check the pair (Membrane of, Interface with).
(any) – gray The measured cells hardly carry the marker (below 25 % of the brightest cell type), so their enrichment is not informative.
Technical: the marker check, exactly

Every cell gets a free-membrane intensity: the mean of its membrane profile where its neighbor track shows no cell (background-subtracted). Without the membrane analysis, the mean of the whole cell is used instead. Measured and partners are the medians of this intensity over the cells of each selection. The brightest cell type is the highest median over the cell types and immune subtypes, excluding artefacts. The rules are applied in this order:

  1. partners / measured ≥ 125 %: brighter on the partners (red);
  2. measured below 25 % of the brightest cell type: not informative (gray);
  3. 80–125 %: on both (amber);
  4. 25–80 %: the partners carry part (amber);
  5. below 25 %: mainly on the measured cells (green).

These limits are rules of thumb. At 25 %, the partner adds a quarter of the measured cell's membrane signal to every interface pixel it reaches. At 80–125 %, an interface between two equally stained membranes looks like a doubling, whatever the biology.

If the badge is amber or red, you can choose the pair the other way round (if the marker is on the partners), use log2 ratio above same-type contacts, compare with a pair whose partners do not carry the marker, or treat the result as an upper limit.

Look at the subsets, on both sides. The default pair (all cells of the type that carries the marker, with all cells of the other type) can hide an effect that only one subset shows. In one test, a receptor that was strongly polarized on A+ immune cells gave a median of only 0.2 SD over all immune cells, and a ligand that was enriched only where B+ cells touched gave 0.7 SD with all immune cells. The All pairs table in the dashboard and Membrane pairs.tsv give every combination of Membrane of and Interface with at once. Read them before you conclude that there is no enrichment.

Technical: inside only, and why it is no cure

Straighten inside the measured cell only reads the band only where it lies inside the measured cell, so that it does not reach into the partner. This is a sensitivity test, not a separation. Touching membranes are nanometers apart, far below the resolution of the ImageStream, so the blur mixes both membranes in every pixel near the interface, whichever pixels are read. If the enrichment drops clearly with inside only, part of it may come from the partner side. If it stays the same, that is reassuring but not proof.

Inside only can also cut away the measured cell's own membrane at a contact. The border between two masks need not lie on the membrane, and on real data the measured cells' membrane at a contact lay partly on the partner's side of that border. A drop with inside only is therefore not by itself proof that the signal came from the partner. Across the membrane in the dashboard shows where the membrane lies at the contacts.

Several markers of interest

You can tick more than one channel as MOI on the import page (channels.marker_of_interest is a list). Every marker of interest is analyzed in the same way, on the same outlines and neighbor tracks. Each marker gets its own pair: by default, the cell type that carries that marker against the other type. A marker on the tumor cells and a marker on the immune cells are therefore each measured on the cells that carry them.

All markers of interest are treated alike, also when there is only one: the name of the marker is part of the names of its files and columns. The membrane files get " - " and the name before the extension, for example Membrane intensity analysis - Marker.tsv. The per-event columns and the overview columns get the name in brackets, for example mean tumor interface (Marker). Membrane pairs.tsv stays one file, with the marker in its first column. See The output folder.

In the dashboard, the menu Marker in the membrane card switches between the markers. The comparison of conditions tests each marker separately (see Comparing conditions).

The per-event table

Independently of the profiles, every event gets the mean of each marker of interest at the interface and on the rest of the membrane, for each cell type. These values are in All cell combinations.tsv, and for the events with one tumor cell and one immune cell also in Single Tumor Single Immune cell.tsv, as in the macro. They are measured in the membrane band of each cell type (Membrane / interface width), not in the straightened profiles.

This is the macro's measure, and it has none of the safeguards described above. It takes all partners of the other type together, has no control, and does not follow the chosen membrane pair. A partner that carries the marker, or two stained membranes side by side, raise it as much as a real enrichment does (in a test without any enrichment it was 1.27). The overview column median … membrane ratio, doublets shows this measure for the cell type that carries the marker, and the dashboard shows it in the Events table and in the sort membrane ratio per event. Read it together with the marker check, and base your conclusions on the pair comparisons.

pages.title: Comparing conditions
pages.html:
Does a treatment change which immune cells touch the tumor cells, or how strongly a marker gathers at the interface? The overview answers such questions with a test across replicates, the independent units of the experiment (usually donors). It compares two measures between conditions:

  • the subset preference: the ratio observed / expected of the contacts of each immune subtype with tumor cells and with the other subtypes;
  • the membrane enrichment: the median enrichment (the log2 ratio of interface and free membrane) of every membrane pair of the cell type that carries the marker with the other cell type. With several markers of interest, each marker is a measure of its own, for example membrane enrichment (Marker).

Labeling the datasets

In the dataset tables of the import page (step 2), give each dataset that should take part in the comparison:

  • a Condition, for example control or treated. Datasets without a condition do not take part.
  • a Replicate: the donor, or the independent experiment, that the dataset comes from. Give the control sample and the treated sample of one donor the same replicate. The comparison is then made within each donor (paired). Datasets without a replicate are left out, and the overview lists them.

Several datasets with the same condition and the same replicate (for example two tubes from one donor) are pooled into one. They are technical repeats, not replicates: only independent units count as replicates.

You can set or change the labels after the analysis. The overview updates at once, and Save settings writes condition comparison.tsv again. On the command line, imagestream-cli overview <project folder> does the same.

Classify the conditions together. Otherwise a subtype can differ between conditions only because its threshold differs. Give the datasets that you compare one experiment label, so that they are classified together, or set the thresholds by hand. The overview warns you when the datasets you compare were classified separately.

Reading the result

The section Comparing conditions of the overview compares each condition with the reference condition, which you choose under Compare with. By default, the reference is the first condition in the project. The section first states how the comparison was made:

  • paired, when two or more replicates have both conditions. Replicates that have only one of the two conditions are left out.
  • unpaired, when the conditions come from different replicates, with two or more replicates for each condition.
  • no test, in all other cases. The values of each replicate are then shown without a test.

Below this, the section has one table per measure. Each table lists the pairs that could be tested, the most significant first:

Column Meaning
ratio (condition / reference) For the subset preference: observed / expected in the condition, divided by observed / expected in the reference. A value above 1 means that these cells touch more often after the treatment.
difference (log2 ratio) For the membrane enrichment: the median log2 ratio in the condition minus that in the reference. +1 means that the enrichment doubled; for example from 1.5 to 3 times as bright as the free membrane.
95% interval The range that contains the true change with 95 % confidence, judged from the spread between the replicates.
p The probability of a change at least this large between the replicates if the conditions did not differ.
q p corrected for the number of pairs tested. A pair with q below 0.05 is shown in bold.
Per replicate The value of each replicate, as reference → condition. Check whether the change goes in the same direction in every replicate.
Note Why a pair was not tested, the result of the marker check of a membrane pair, or a warning about the classification.

A pair is not tested when any replicate has fewer than 5 expected contacts (subset preference) or fewer than 10 cells with an interface (membrane enrichment). condition comparison.tsv also lists these pairs, with the reason.

Read q, not p. When ten or more pairs are tested, one of them usually has a p below 0.05 by chance alone. q keeps the probability of any false finding near 5 %.

Few replicates give little power. The test judges a change by how consistent it is between the replicates, so two replicates rarely give a significant result, even when the change is real. With two replicates the interval is wide, because the test has only one degree of freedom. Changes in contact preference are small, because few events give an immune cell a choice of partner. In simulations of such a change, experiments with three donors and 300 events per sample detected it in about one experiment in ten, and experiments with four donors and 3000 events per sample in three out of four (see the calibration below). With few replicates, a result that is not significant is no evidence that nothing changed. Look at the interval instead: it shows which changes are still possible.

Why there is no test per donor

The subset preference of each dataset has a 95 % interval, which reflects the sampling of its events. Even when the intervals of two samples from one donor do not overlap, this does not show that the treatment had an effect. Two samples of the same cells differ by more than the sampling of their events, for example through the preparation, the staining or the gate in IDEAS. In simulations, a test of one donor's two samples against each other reported a difference in up to three out of four comparisons in which there was none. The tool therefore tests only across replicates, where this variation is part of the error.

Technical: the comparison, exactly

Units. Each combination of a replicate and a condition is one unit. For the subset preference, the observed contacts O and the expected contacts E of a pair (subtype S and a partner) are summed over the datasets of the unit. The value of the unit is y = lnbig((O + 0.5) / (E + 0.5)big): the log of observed / expected, with 0.5 added to both so that a pair without contacts still has a value. Each immune–immune pair is tested once, because S–T and T–S are the same contacts. For the membrane enrichment, the value of the unit is the median log2 ratio of its datasets, weighted by their numbers of cells with an interface (until 2026-11-05: the median SD above mean; results of older versions have no log2 ratio and must be run again). Only the pairs of the cell type that carries the marker with the other cell type are tested (Membrane of that type or one of its subsets, and Interface with the other cell type or one of its subsets). The pairs within one cell type are controls, not hypotheses. Each marker of interest is tested on its own, and the cell type that carries it comes from the column marker on of each dataset's Membrane pairs.tsv. A pair set for the marker (for example the tumor cells against Subtype A+ cells) is in that file too, and is tested when it measures that type against the other. When the datasets disagree, the type named by most of them is used, and a note on every row of that marker says so. Results from before November 2026 lack this column; run the analysis again to compare them. Testing several markers does not change the test itself: the q values are adjusted within each measure, as for one marker.

Paired (two or more replicates with both conditions): for each replicate the difference is $d_i = y_i^{\,\mathrm{cond}} - y_i^{\,\mathrm{ref}}, and a one-sample t-test compares the mean\bar d$ with 0, with n - 1 degrees of freedom. The interval is bar d pm t0.975, n-1 sd / sqrt n. For the subset preference, the effect and its interval are shown as ratios: ebar d is the geometric mean, over the replicates, of the ratio of the two observed / expected values. Unpaired (in all other cases, with two or more replicates per condition): Welch's t-test compares the means of y, with the Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. q: the Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment over the pairs tested for one measure and one condition.

Eligibility. A pair is tested only when every unit of the comparison has E ge 5 (subset preference) or at least 10 cells with an interface (membrane enrichment). Otherwise, its note names the units that fall short. The test needs at least two replicates on each side. With exactly two, the t distribution has one degree of freedom, and t0.975 = 12.7.

What the test assumes. The replicates are independent, and the differences per replicate (on the log scale for the subset preference) are roughly normally distributed. Datasets from one donor that are labeled as different replicates violate the first assumption and make the test too liberal. The test tells whether the conditions differ in the cells that were exported. The selection in IDEAS and the size of the subtypes affect both conditions, and their effects cancel only when they are the same in both.

Not independent. The subset preferences within one dataset are linked: when one subtype takes more of the contacts with tumor cells, the other subtypes take fewer. A real change in one subtype therefore also shows up as a smaller, opposite change in the others, so read the pairs together.

Technical: calibration by simulation

The tests were checked on simulated experiments with a known truth (tools/stats/calibrate_comparison.py in the repository, which takes about 4 minutes). The events were made with the geometry of the synthetic test data: one or two tumor cells and up to three immune cells of five subtypes, placed touching each other at random, except that a cell of subtype A was placed next to a tumor cell with probability pA. The donors differed (pA = 0.4, with an SD of 0.1 between donors), and each sample had 150–3000 events. Only the contacts were simulated, not the images. In this geometry, pA = 0.4 gives a true A–tumor preference of 1.07, and pA = 0.95 gives one of 1.12.

No difference between the conditions (the proportion of experiments with p < 0.05; 2000 experiments each, so the proportions are accurate to ±0.01):

donors paired unpaired (Welch) paired, samples differ (SD 0.05 on y)
2 0.053 0.024 0.057
3 0.049 0.030 0.043
4 0.044 0.036 0.059
6 0.049 0.047 0.044

The paired test keeps its error rate at 5 %, also when the samples differ by more than the sampling of their events. Welch's test is conservative when there are few replicates.

A test of one donor's two samples against each other (z = the difference divided by its standard error from the events, estimated by the jackknife over events), with no true difference; the table shows the proportion of comparisons with |z| > 1.96:

SD between two samples of a donor, on y 300 events 3000 events
0 0.060 0.048
0.03 0.066 0.364
0.05 0.178 0.512
0.10 0.398 0.754

This test is correct only when two samples of a donor differ in nothing but their events, which cannot be checked. The more events, the worse it gets. This is why the tool has no test per donor.

All subset pairs at once (with no difference anywhere), the probability of at least one finding:

donors, events per sample pairs tested (mean) any p < 0.05 any q < 0.05
3, 300 5.3 0.20 0.053
4, 1000 14.7 0.51 0.058
6, 300 4.3 0.19 0.049

Power: subtype A was placed next to a tumor cell with probability 0.4 in the control and 0.95 after the treatment (a true preference of 1.07 → 1.12). The table shows the proportion of experiments with p < 0.05:

events per sample 2 donors 3 4 6 10
300 0.06 0.11 0.16 0.28 0.50
1000 0.09 0.23 0.39 0.65 0.93
3000 0.18 0.47 0.74 0.96 1.00

A cell type that is placed next to the tumor cell more than twice as often changes observed / expected by only 4 %, because most events offer little choice. Keep this in mind when you plan the number of donors and events.

Membrane enrichment: the scores per cell (the test does not depend on their unit) were drawn from a skewed distribution (a normal core, with a quarter of the cells in an exponential tail), with 10–200 cells with an interface per sample and donors that differed. With no difference between the conditions, the paired test of the medians gave p < 0.05 in 0.043–0.053 of the experiments, with 2–6 donors.

pages.title: All settings
pages.html:
This page lists every setting as it is written in a settings file or in project.toml ([section], then name = value). For each setting it gives the default and, if the setting appears on the import page, its label there. A channel can be given by its number or by its name.

[input]

The input: the IDEAS export or the stack, the dataset, its channels and its pixel size.

Setting Default On the import page Meaning
image (none) The input file: an IDEAS export (.zip, with one folder per dataset) or an ImageJ hyperstack made by ImageStreamCombiner (.tif, with one frame per event).
output 'output' The results are written to a folder inside this folder, named after the dataset (or the stack).
max_events (empty) Only the first N events (empty = all) Analyze only the first N events (in order of object number). Empty means all events.
dataset (empty) IDEAS zip only: the dataset to analyze (a folder in the zip). Empty means the only dataset in the zip.
channels [] IDEAS zip only: the channels to load, as IDEAS channel numbers (Ch<N>). Channels that have a role are always loaded.
channel_names [] IDEAS zip only: the names of these channels, in the same order as in channels.
pixel_size (empty) The pixel size in µm per pixel. It is required for an IDEAS zip, because the files in the zip do not record it.

[channels]

The role of each channel, given by channel number or by channel name.

Setting Default On the import page Meaning
brightfield 1 The brightfield channel.
marker_of_interest [2] The markers whose enrichment at the interface is measured, as a list. Every marker is analyzed in the same way, and its columns and files carry its name. Empty ([]) means no marker of interest: the tool then determines only the cell types and their contacts. The membrane analysis needs at least one marker of interest.
tumor 3 The tumor-cell marker.
immune [4] The immune-cell marker or markers, as a list. With several markers, each is normalized and the results are summed (the phenotypic markers of macro 2.8).
functional [] The immune subtype markers, as a list. Each immune cell is called positive or negative for each of them (the functional markers of macro 2.8).
marker_location 'nuclear' Tumor / immune markers Where the tumor and immune markers stain: "nuclear" (the nucleus or the cytoplasm) or "membrane". This determines the image that Cellpose 3 segments. Cellpose 4 (model cpsam) gets every segmentation channel on its own (brightfield variance, tumor marker, immune markers), so this setting does not matter there.

[segmentation]

Cellpose, and the clean-up of the cells it finds.

Setting Default On the import page Meaning
method 'cellpose' "cellpose" runs Cellpose. "labelmap" loads the labels from labelmap_file instead.
labelmap_file (empty) The labelmap_cells.tif (or the Fiji macro's .zip) of an earlier run.
model 'cyto3' Model (cyto3, cpsam, or a path) The Cellpose model: cyto3, cyto2, nuclei, and so on for Cellpose 3, or cpsam for Cellpose 4. It can also be the path of a model file.
diameter 30.0 Cell diameter (px) The typical cell diameter in pixels. 0 means that Cellpose estimates it (Cellpose 3 only).
flow_threshold 0.5 The flow threshold of Cellpose. A higher value gives more cells, some of them less certain.
cellprob_threshold 0.0 The cell probability threshold of Cellpose. A lower value gives larger cells.
use_gpu true Use the GPU Run Cellpose on the GPU.
reuse_labels true Reuse the previous Cellpose result if nothing changed Reuse the Cellpose result of the previous run of the dataset if its input image and Cellpose settings have not changed (labelmap_cells.tif and its .json file in the dataset folder). When off, Cellpose always runs.
montage_columns 0 Montage columns (0 = square) The number of events per row in the montage that Cellpose segments. 0 makes the montage about square. Setting it to the number of events gives a single row, as in the Fiji macro.
cellpose_python (empty) Python with Cellpose The python.exe of an environment with Cellpose 3 or 4, or the folder of that environment (a venv, conda or pixi environment, or a project folder with .venv or .pixi). Empty means the environment of this program.
erosion 1 Shrink cells (px) Shrink the cells by this many pixels at their border with the background.
min_cell_size 100 Min. cell size (px) Cells smaller than this (in pixels, after shrinking) are removed.
max_cell_size 10000 Max. cell size (px) Cells larger than this (in pixels, after shrinking) are removed.
exclude_edge_cells false Leave out cells cut by the image edge Leave out cells that are cut by the edge of their event image. Such cells are always flagged in the column Edge, whether or not they are left out.

[classification]

The thresholds of the subtype markers, artefacts and pools.

Setting Default On the import page Meaning
threshold_method 'Two populations' Threshold of the subtype markers The method for the automatic threshold of the subtype markers, applied to log(intensity - min + 1). "Two populations" puts the threshold where a cell is as likely to belong to the positive population as to the negative one; when there is no second population, it uses the upper noise limit of the negative cells. "MaxEntropy" works as in macro 2.8. "MaxEntropy strict" raises the MaxEntropy threshold, if needed, to at least 2 robust SDs above the negative cells. "Otsu" is the fourth choice. A settings file also accepts "Yen" and "RenyiEntropy".
thresholds {} Thresholds set by hand (Apply in a dashboard) Thresholds set by hand, by marker name, for example { "Subtype A" = 12.5 }, as background-subtracted intensities. They replace the automatic thresholds.
artefact_min_positive (empty) Artefact: positive in at least N subtype markers (0 = none) A detection that is positive in at least this many subtype markers is an artefact, not a cell. Empty means all subtype markers (only with two or more of them). 0 means that no detection is an artefact.
pool 'experiment' Classify together (one set of thresholds) In a project, "experiment" classifies the datasets of each experiment together, with one set of thresholds. "dataset" classifies each dataset on its own.

[membrane]

The membrane profiles and the enrichment at the interface.

Setting Default On the import page Meaning
analysis false Membrane profiles and enrichment Measure the membrane profiles and the enrichment at the interface. The interface table per event is always made, whether or not this is on.
cells [] The cells whose membrane is measured, as a list. Each item is a cell type ("Tumor", "Immune"), an immune subtype as written in the tables ("Immune A+ B+"), or a marker ("A+" means the immune cells positive for A). Empty means the cell type that carries the marker of interest, decided per marker from the data (the median intensity of the membrane that touches no cell). Set here, it applies to every marker of interest without an entry of its own in pairs (the import page writes pairs only).
partners [] The partners whose contact forms the interface, written as for cells. Empty means the other cell type.
pairs {} Membrane pair per marker of interest The pair of each marker of interest, by marker name, for example { Marker = { cells = ['Tumor'], partners = ['B+'] } }. A side that an entry leaves out comes from cells or partners above, and else is automatic.
thickness (empty) Membrane / interface width (px) In pixels: the width of the membrane band, which is also the distance at which cells count as touching. Empty means about 1.5 µm (2 px at 20x, 3 px at 40x, 5 px at 60x).
straightening_width (empty) Straightening width (px) In pixels: the width of the band across the outline that is straightened. Empty means about 4.5 µm (5 px at 20x, 9 px at 40x, 13 px at 60x). This width lets the band reach the membrane where the outline lies a little outside it.
band_centre 'membrane' Band centred on Where the band across the membrane is centred. "membrane": where the membrane lies, found in the data: per cell type, the marker of interest averaged across the outline, separately at the free membrane and at the contacts with each cell type. "cell": the same, but every cell's free membrane on the peak of its own (cells differ from each other), its contacts moved by as much plus the type's difference between contact and free membrane; cells with too little free membrane, or without a clear peak, as "membrane". "outline": on the outline, as macro 1.8. The outline lies outside a free membrane (about 1 µm) but on the contact line where cells touch, so a band on the outline reaches less of the free membrane than of an interface, and an interface can look enriched without cause.
max_histogram_value (empty) Histogram maximum (SD) The upper end of the histograms, in SD above the mean. The histograms start at -5. Empty means automatic: the 99th percentile of the interface values or of the control windows, whichever is higher (at least 5), rounded up to a whole number of bins. Values above the upper end are not counted.
histogram_bin_width (empty) Histogram bin width (SD) The bin width of the histograms, in SD. Empty means automatic: the smallest of 0.1, 0.2, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10, ... that gives at most 60 bins (usually 25 to 60).
control_repeats 10 Control windows per cell The number of random control windows per cell without an interface. Each window is as long as the median interface.
inside_only false Straighten inside the measured cell only Take the profile only from the part of the band that lies inside the measured cell. This is a sensitivity test, not a way to separate the two membranes: touching membranes are much closer together than the resolution, so every pixel at the interface contains signal from both.

pages.title: Settings files and the command line
pages.html:
Everything that the import page does can also be done from a terminal. You then use either a project file, for several exports, or a settings file, for one dataset. Both are TOML text files.

Commands

uv run imagestream-cli gui                          # the import page (also: uv run imagestream)
uv run imagestream-cli shortcut                     # a shortcut to the import page on the Desktop and in the Start menu
uv run imagestream-cli run-project D:\data\project  # all datasets of a project (project.toml or its folder)
uv run imagestream-cli run-project D:\data\project --dataset "Donor 2"   # only this dataset (repeat for several)
uv run imagestream-cli overview D:\data\project     # rewrite the overview tables, without analyzing (after new conditions)
uv run imagestream-cli run settings.toml            # one dataset, with a settings file
uv run imagestream-cli run settings.toml --max-events 50
uv run imagestream-cli example-settings > settings.toml   # a settings file with every default

With --dataset, run-project runs only the named datasets; the others keep their results, and the overview is written again from all of them. With pools per experiment (classification.pool = "experiment"), the other datasets of the same experiment run too, because they are classified together.

A settings file

A settings file describes one dataset. It has the sections [input], [channels], [segmentation], [classification] and [membrane]. Relative paths are taken relative to the folder of the settings file. An unknown setting is an error, so that a typing error is not silently ignored. All settings lists every setting.

[input]
image = 'D:/data/example_export.zip'
dataset = 'Donor 1'
channels = [1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8]
channel_names = ['BF', 'Marker', 'Tumor', 'Immune', 'Subtype A', 'Subtype B']
pixel_size = 0.5
output = 'results'

[channels]
brightfield = 'BF'           # a channel by name (or by number: brightfield = 1)
marker_of_interest = ['Marker']  # one or more, or [] for none
tumor = 'Tumor'
immune = ['Immune']
functional = ['Subtype A', 'Subtype B']

[segmentation]
cellpose_python = 'D:/envs/cellpose3/Scripts/python.exe'
diameter = 20.0

[membrane]
analysis = true

Each run writes the complete settings that it used to settings.toml in the folder of the dataset, with the channels given by number. You can use that file to repeat the run exactly.

A project file

The import page writes the project file project.toml. It holds the panel (the [channels] section, with the channels given by name), the settings that all datasets share, and one [[zip]] section for each export, with its datasets:

[channels]
brightfield = 'BF'
marker_of_interest = ['Marker']
tumor = 'Tumor'
immune = ['Immune']
functional = ['Subtype A', 'Subtype B']

[classification]
pool = 'experiment'

[[zip]]
path = 'D:/data/example_export.zip'
pixel_size = 0.5
channels = [1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8]
channel_names = ['BF', 'Marker', 'Tumor', 'Immune', 'Subtype A', 'Subtype B']

[[zip.dataset]]
name = 'Donor 1'
experiment = 'Example'
include = true
condition = 'control'      # optional, to compare conditions: the condition
replicate = 'Donor 1'      # and the independent unit (donor) it comes from

The reference condition, with which the other conditions are compared, goes in a section of its own. If it is empty or absent, the first condition in the file is used:

[comparison]
reference = 'control'
Technical: older files

Settings files from before November 2026 name the immune marker t_cell = 4; it is read as immune = [4]. They give one marker of interest (marker_of_interest = 2 or 'Marker', or '' for none), which is read as a list ([2], ['Marker'] or []). Their cell_of_interest (Marker of interest expressed in) is ignored with a note in the log: the measured cells now follow from the data (see A pair of cell types). Older project files, which set the roles for each export by channel number, are converted to roles by name when all exports agree (see The import page).

pages.title: From the Fiji macros
pages.html:
ImageStream Analysis for Python is a port of two Fiji macros, which are kept in the legacy/ folder of the repository:

  • Analyze_ImageStream_stack_2celltypes_+_membrane_intensity_analysis_1.8.ijm separates tumor cells and T cells by k-means, measures the interface in each event, and analyzes the membrane enrichment.
  • ClassifyCellTypes_2_8.ijm uses several immune markers, assigns immune subtypes by thresholds, finds the cells that touch, and has a class for detections that are not cells.

The port reads the IDEAS exports directly, so it replaces ImageStreamCombiner. It also combines the two macros: the analysis of macro 1.8 is the special case of one immune marker and no subtype markers. The port was validated against the output of macro 1.8. The cells and the per-event tables match to three decimals, with 100 % agreement on the classes, and the results of the membrane analysis have the same distributions. Where the macros could be improved, the port does not reproduce them exactly. The differences are listed below, and described in detail in docs/SPEC.md in the repository.

Differences

Topic The macros This program Why
Input a Combiner stack the IDEAS zip, with the object numbers kept each cell can be traced back to IDEAS, and there is one step less
Cellpose montage one row of all events a grid that is about square faster, with the same masks
Cells that cross the border between two events in the montage one cell split into one cell per event each event is a separate image
Names T cell immune cell the immune side can be a panel of markers
Immune markers one (1.8); raw values summed (2.8) several, each normalized, then summed markers of different brightness get equal weight
Clustering 1.8: normalized markers and area; 2.8: raw sums, with the functional markers added without normalization as in 1.8 2.8 added the functional markers without normalizing them, which was a mistake
Subtype thresholds MaxEntropy on all cells (2.8) Two populations (or MaxEntropy or Otsu) on the immune cells only tumor cells no longer shift the threshold, and MaxEntropy called noise positive or missed positive cells (see Cell types)
Detections that are not cells a "crap" class, switched off and not working artefacts: detections that are positive in all subtype markers —
Contacts region adjacency graph of the labels cells within the interface width of each other consistent with the interfaces
Contacts compared with chance — partner preference in events with 3 or more cells, and subset preference among immune cells, with intervals new
Membranes one ring per blob of touching cells of the same class one membrane per cell the cell is the unit of analysis
Straightening width 5 px about 4.5 µm (9 px at 40×) 5 px at 40× gave a false enrichment at every contact (see Membrane enrichment)
Place of the band on the outline where the membrane lies, found in the data per cell type, at the free membrane and at the contacts with each cell type (Band centred on: outline gives the macro's) the outline lies outside a free membrane but near the membrane at contacts, which favoured the interface (see Where the membrane lies)

Technical: what is kept exactly

Several steps are the same as in macro 1.8, so that the results stay comparable: the normalization of the markers (the median over the events of the Otsu threshold of each event, computed with ImageJ's 8-bit histogram of float images), the brightfield variance filter (with ImageJ's circular kernel), the erosion and dilation (CLIJ2's 4-connected steps), the k-means features and the rule that picks the tumor cluster, the per-event table, and the doublet table. The ImageJ automatic threshold methods are ported exactly and give the same thresholds as Fiji.

pages.title: Questions and problems
pages.html:
Setting up

The run button stays gray. The list above the button shows what is missing: an output folder, a pixel size, or a channel for one of the roles in one of the exports. A role is a tick box next to a named channel. If a channel in an export has a different name (for example because of a typing difference), it does not get the role.

"Cellpose failed". The log shows Cellpose's own error message. Check Python with Cellpose: it must point to the python.exe, or the folder, of an environment in which Cellpose is installed. The chip next to Segmentation (Cellpose) on the import page shows whether Cellpose and a GPU were found there. If Use the GPU is off, Cellpose runs on the processor, which is much slower.

An export has objects without all channels. IDEAS can export objects with missing channels. These objects are left out, and the log says how many there are. On the import page, the Complete column counts the objects that have all the channels that are needed.

Results

Cells are missed or merged. Check Cell diameter (px) first: Cellpose works best when it matches the size of the cells. If the markers stain the membrane rather than the cytoplasm, set Tumor / immune markers to membrane. Changing Montage columns does not make much difference; leave it at 0.

Tumor and immune cells are swapped, or mixed. The k-means clustering needs both cell types to be present, and markers that separate them. Look at Cell classes in the dashboard, where two separate clouds should be visible. If there are very few cells of one type, the clustering may split the other type into two instead.

There are many artefacts. The automatic thresholds are liberal, so real cells can be positive in all subtype markers by chance. Look at the histograms in the dashboard. Then try MaxEntropy strict, set the thresholds by hand, or, if the artefact rule was set to fewer than all subtype markers, raise that number (0 switches the rule off). See Cell types.

A rare subtype appears that should not exist (for example A+ C+ in a few cells). The automatic threshold of one of the markers probably lies within the noise of the negative cells. Look at the histogram of that marker in the dashboard, drag the slider into the gap between the two peaks, and click Apply to the project…. See Cell types.

I only want cell types and contacts. Leave the MOI role unticked and Membrane profiles and enrichment off. The run then does not need a marker of interest.

I have several markers of interest. Tick MOI for each of them. Each is measured on the cell type that carries it, and the dashboard's membrane card gets a Marker menu. See Several markers of interest.

Does a subtype prefer the tumor cells? Look at the among immune cells tab of the Interactions card in the dashboard. It compares the subtypes with each other within events, with a 95 % interval. See Cell contacts.

The partner preference is close to 1 everywhere. Most contacts may be in events of only two cells. Such events cannot show a preference and are left out; the dashboard says how many pairs remain. If there are few events of three or more cells, the ratios are uncertain. See Cell contacts.

The membrane badge is amber or red. The partner cells carry the marker of interest too, so the interface may show their membrane rather than that of the measured cells. By default the measured cells are the type that carries the marker, so a red badge means that Membrane of or Interface with was set by hand. See Where the marker is expressed.

The control is not centered on 0. The control windows score random stretches of free membrane. If the staining is uneven along the membrane, the control values spread out. The comparison that matters is the interface against the control of the same dataset.

The numbers differ slightly between two runs. The control windows are placed at random (without a seed); everything else is the same when the settings are the same. The control in the dashboard uses a fixed seed.

The dashboard

The dashboard is slow with many events. Only the events that are visible are drawn, but the plots draw every cell. Filter the events, or analyze fewer events (Only the first N events) while you test settings.

Can I send a dashboard to a colleague? Yes. Send the folder of the dataset (dashboard.html together with dashboard_files/). It opens in any modern browser, without the program and without an internet connection.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.html:
Artefact
A detection that is positive in all subtype markers (or in at least N of them) and is therefore taken not to be a cell. Artefacts are left out of the clustering and out of the cell counts.
Background
For each channel, the median, over all objects, of the median intensity of each object. The background is subtracted from the mean intensities of the cells.
Dataset
A folder in an IDEAS export, which holds the objects of one sample. Each dataset is analyzed into a folder of its own.
Event
One object recorded by the ImageStream: one image that contains one or more cells.
Experiment
A label that groups datasets. Datasets with the same experiment label are classified together (as one pool), and their contacts are pooled in the overview's partner-preference matrix.
Free membrane
The part of a cell's membrane that touches no other cell. It is the baseline for the enrichment.
Interface
The part of a cell's membrane that lies within the interface width (Membrane / interface width) of a partner cell.
Marker of interest (MOI)
A marker whose enrichment at the interface is measured. A panel can have several, which are all analyzed alike. By default, each is measured on the cell type that carries it.
Neighbor track
For every position along a cell's membrane, the cell that touches it at that position (or none).
Partner preference
The number of contacts between two cell types that is observed, divided by the number expected by chance, in events of three or more cells.
Pool
A group of datasets that are classified together, with one clustering and one set of thresholds.
Project
The exports, the channel names and roles, and the settings, saved as project.toml, together with the results of all datasets.
Subtype marker
A marker (with the role Subtype) that is scored as positive or negative in each immune cell. The positive markers give the subtype its name.
Touching
Two cells in the same event are touching when they lie within the interface width of each other.
